Also Neptune is so far from the sun that it is freezing, and one year on Neptune is about a hundred and sixty five Earth years. So you would never have a birthday. That is the worst part. I just had my birthday yesterday and I would not want to wait that long.
entries.highlight: Imagined a school on Neptune and figured out that its long year means you would almost never have a birthday.

entries.title: Saturn would float in a bathtub
entries.body: Today I thought about what school would be like on Saturn again. Last April I said recess would be in the rings and you could slide on them. Now I know more. The rings are made of chunks of ice and rock, some as small as sand and some as big as a house. So sliding would not work, you would get bonked. Also Saturn is less dense than water, so if you had a bathtub big enough, Saturn would float in it! I wonder who had a bathtub big enough to test it. I told Dad and he said I did not know that. That made me feel smart. School on Saturn would float, so my old idea was a little bit right.
entries.highlight: Revisited his idea of a school on Saturn with new facts about its rings and the fact that Saturn would float in water.

entries.title: A real book about the space station
entries.body: It was library day and I got a book about the space station from the grown-up section of the school library. It is a lot of words and only some pictures but I can read it. The librarian said it is a fifth grade book. The space station goes around Earth sixteen times a day! So the astronauts see sixteen sunrises every day. I wonder when they go to sleep. There is also a page about the space toilet and it uses a fan to suck everything in. Arjun thought that was the funniest thing ever. I read half of it already. I am going to use it for my space food machine too.
entries.favorite: The page about the space toilet
entries.highlight: Checked out a fifth-grade level book about the space station and shared facts about its sixteen daily sunrises.

entries.title: A new idea for the comic ending
entries.body: I figured out the ending of my comic, finally. In August I thought maybe Bolts should save the day because he was the one who got saved at the beginning. So that is what happens. The moon lab gets hit by a meteor and the air starts leaking out. Captain Crater gets stuck. Bolts uses his claw arm, the one Captain Crater gave him, to fix the hole. It is like a circle. Mr. Brooks said that is called a full circle ending and good writers do that. I have to redraw some pages because my old drawings look too little-kid now.
entries.highlight: Figured out his comic's ending where the robot Bolts saves the hero, and Mr. Brooks called it a full circle ending.

entries.title: Cabbage water for Ivy
entries.body: I needed ingredients for the red cabbage experiment again so me and Mom went to the store on Sunday. This time it is for Ivy. I want to show her the color change like I did in February. I made a list. Red cabbage, lemons, and white vinegar, and we already have baking soda. I let Ivy push the cart. She wanted to buy a purple cabbage and a green one and I said only purple works because of the color stuff inside it. Mom said it is called anthocyanin. I cannot say that word yet. Ivy said it was ant cyan. Close enough.
entries.highlight: Shopped with Mom and Ivy for red cabbage to show his sister a color-changing experiment.

entries.title: Showing the rainbow glass at school
entries.body: Mr. Brooks let me show the rainbow in a glass to the class during science time, because we are learning about liquids. I brought the sugar water already mixed in jars and I used my dropper. I told everyone you have to go slow or it all mixes together and turns brown. I said that happened to me last March. I put the heaviest one at the bottom and the lightest one on top. The whole class went ooh. Mr. Brooks asked why the layers stay and I said because of density, and the more sugar the heavier. I did not even get nervous.
entries.highlight: Demonstrated a layered sugar water rainbow to his third grade class and explained density without getting nervous.

entries.title: Chalk pastel planets in art
entries.body: Today in art we learned something new. We used chalk pastels and you smudge them with your finger to blend. It was hard at first because my fingers got so dusty and everything smeared. But then I got it. I made Neptune with three blues blended together, light and dark. Ms. Green the art teacher said it looked like it had weather. I said it does, it has the fastest winds in the solar system. She did not know that. My fingers were blue until lunch. Hazel made a sunset and it was really pretty.
entries.highlight: Learned to blend chalk pastels in art class and made a stormy Neptune.

entries.title: One month of the moon journal
entries.body: Tonight was a whole month of my moon journal. I missed four nights because of clouds but I have twenty four drawings. It went from nothing, to a skinny crescent, to half, to full, and then back down. My prediction was right but only half right, because I forgot it gets smaller again after it is full. When I look at all the drawings in a row it looks exactly like the lamp and ball model me and Dad did in May. The light just moves across. I showed Mr. Brooks a picture of the pages on Mom's phone and he said that is real scientific observation.
entries.favorite: Seeing it match my lamp model
entries.highlight: Completed a full month of his moon journal and saw the phases match the lamp model he made with Dad.

entries.title: The car ride word game
entries.body: On the ride to school everybody was singing and talking. Then Hazel made up a game where you have to say a science word for every letter of the alphabet. A is asteroid. B is black hole. C is crater. I got stuck on Q, so Hazel said quartz. Wes kept poking me when I was thinking. Annoying but funny. When we got to X, nobody knew. Then I said X-ray and everybody said no fair, but it is a real thing. Hazel said I win the X round. We are going to play it every day until we can do the whole alphabet fast.
entries.favorite: Hazel getting a hard space word
entries.highlight: Played Hazel's science alphabet game on the ride to school and won the X round with X-ray.

entries.title: Orbit means falling around Earth
entries.body: We watched a real rocket launch on the computer after school. I asked Dad why the space station does not fall down. He said it is falling, all the time, but it is going so fast sideways that it keeps missing the Earth. That is called an orbit. I did not believe him so I asked Mr. Brooks the next morning and he said your dad is right. Then he threw a ball across the classroom to show me. If you could throw it fast enough, it would go all the way around. I wonder how fast that is. That is the most interesting thing I learned this year so far.
entries.highlight: Learned from Dad and Mr. Brooks that an orbit means falling around Earth while moving fast sideways.

entries.title: Saturn drawn the right size
entries.body: I drew a picture of Saturn but I did it the real way this time. I looked at the size of the rings in my book and measured with a ruler. The rings are a lot wider than I used to draw them. I always drew them like a skinny ring like a hula hoop. They are actually way wider than the planet. I did the pastels like in art class and blended the tan colors. Then I drew the Cassini gap, which is a dark line between the rings. Mom said this is going on the fridge, and she moved my old Saturn into the drawer with my other old drawings.
entries.favorite: Measuring the rings with a ruler
entries.highlight: Drew Saturn to scale using measurements from his book, including the Cassini gap between its rings.

entries.title: Pumpkins for a pumpkin volcano
entries.body: I needed ingredients for a pumpkin volcano so me and Mom went to the store after school. It is like the baking soda volcano but inside a pumpkin with a face, so the foam comes out of its mouth like it is throwing up. I made a list. A pumpkin, two boxes of baking soda, a big jug of vinegar, dish soap, and green food coloring. I picked the ugliest pumpkin because it will look the grossest. Mom said the dish soap makes the bubbles last longer. I want to test that with one with soap and one without. That is a fair test.
entries.highlight: Shopped with Mom for a Halloween pumpkin volcano and planned a fair test of whether dish soap makes the foam last.

entries.title: Glow sticks in hot and cold water
entries.body: I got glow sticks at the store and did an experiment. I snapped three of them and put one in ice water, one in room temperature water, and one in hot water from the sink. My hypothesis was the hot one would be the brightest. I was right! The hot one was super bright and the cold one was really dim. But then the hot one stopped glowing first, and the cold one lasted all night. Dad said heat makes the chemical reaction go faster. So it is bright but it uses itself up. I wrote that in my notebook with a little drawing of each one.
entries.highlight: Tested glow sticks in hot, room temperature and cold water and found heat makes the reaction brighter but shorter.

entries.title: Planning Halloween with Arjun
entries.body: Arjun came over after school and we planned our Halloween costumes. I want to be an astronaut with a cardboard jetpack. Arjun is going to be an alien so we match. We made a list of what we need: two soda bottles for the jetpack, silver paint, tape, and straps from an old backpack. Arjun said I should have red streamers coming out the bottom like fire. That is a great idea. Then we did experiments with my glow sticks from my lab, and Arjun said we could put them in his alien antennas. Lab partners forever, and costume partners forever too.
entries.favorite: Arjun's idea for streamers like fire
entries.highlight: Planned matching astronaut and alien Halloween costumes with Arjun, including a cardboard jetpack.

entries.title: A Halloween page for Blip
entries.body: After Arjun went home I drew a bonus page for my comic. It is a Halloween special. Blip the alien wants to go trick or treating but he does not need a costume, because he already looks like an alien. So everybody thinks he is a kid in a really good costume and gives him extra candy. Bolts dresses up as a toaster. Captain Crater goes as a regular human. I made a speech bubble where Blip says can I join and the kids say yes. I like that Blip always says can I join. It is kind of his thing now.
entries.highlight: Drew a Halloween bonus page for his comic where Blip the alien goes trick-or-treating without a costume.

entries.title: Ivy did the cabbage experiment herself
entries.body: Today I taught Ivy how to do the cabbage water experiment all by herself. Last February I would not even let her in my lab. Now she has her own goggles that fit. I made her a little card with pictures instead of words because she cannot read yet. Picture one, pour purple water. Picture two, add lemon, it turns pink. Picture three, add baking soda, it turns blue. She did every step and I only helped her hold the cup once. When it turned pink she yelled I did it like a scientist. It was the best feeling. I think I like being a teacher.
entries.favorite: Ivy saying I did it like a scientist
entries.highlight: Taught Ivy to do the red cabbage experiment on her own using a picture card he made for her.

entries.title: Building the jetpack with Arjun
entries.body: There was no school today, so Arjun came over and we built my jetpack. We taped two soda bottles together and painted them silver in the garage. Then we glued the straps from the old backpack. We put red and orange streamers at the bottom so it looks like fire. The tape was not strong enough for the straps so Dad gave us the duct tape. Arjun's alien antennas are pipe cleaners with glow sticks taped on top. We tested it by running around the yard. One streamer fell off. We said it is just a tiny engine failure.
entries.highlight: Built his cardboard and bottle jetpack costume with Arjun on a day off from school.

entries.title: The moon rising late
entries.body: Dad and me looked at the stars from the backyard with my new red flashlight. It was cool but not cold. I wanted to draw the moon for my journal but it was not up yet. Dad said after the full moon, the moon rises later and later every night. It is because the moon moves along its orbit a little every day. So we waited, and it came up over the trees really orange and big. Dad said it only looks bigger near the trees. It is called the moon illusion. I drew it in my journal and wrote the time, nine forty.
entries.highlight: Waited with Dad for a late-rising moon and learned about the moon illusion while using his new red flashlight.

entries.title: I invented planet tag
entries.body: At recess I invented a new tag game called planet tag. Whoever is it is the sun. If the sun tags you, you have to orbit around the slide one time before you can run again. And if you get tagged three times you become Pluto and you have to stand at the far fence because you are a dwarf planet now. Everybody wanted to be Pluto for some reason. A second grader came over and said can I join and we said yes. Then two more came. Mr. Brooks said it was the most scientific recess game he has ever seen.
entries.highlight: Invented a recess game called planet tag that drew in younger kids, and Mr. Brooks called it scientific.

entries.title: Pumpkin patch with Felix
entries.body: On Sunday we drove to the pumpkin patch and Felix came with us. In the car we played the science alphabet game from the school ride and Felix got stuck on Z. I said zero gravity. Felix said zebra is not a science word and I said animals are biology, so yes it is. At the pumpkin patch there was a hay maze and a pumpkin that weighed four hundred pounds. Felix said if we hollowed it out we could live in it. I said we could make it a pumpkin volcano. Felix said a giant one. Then we got lost in the maze and Dad had to yell so we could follow his voice out.
entries.highlight: Went to the pumpkin patch with Felix, played the science alphabet game in the car, and got lost in the hay maze.

entries.title: A feather and a ball falling
entries.body: Today in science we learned about gravity. Mr. Brooks dropped a ball and a piece of paper at the same time and the ball hit first. Then he crumpled the paper and dropped them again and they hit at the same time! He said air pushes on the flat paper and slows it down. Then he showed us a video of an astronaut on the moon dropping a hammer and a feather. They hit the ground at the same time because the moon has no air. I raised my hand and said that is why the footprints are still on the moon too, no air and no wind. I wonder how long they will last.
entries.favorite: Mr. Brooks showing the moon video
entries.highlight: Learned in science class that objects fall at the same rate without air resistance and connected it to footprints on the moon.

entries.title: Pumpkin carving with Arjun
entries.body: Arjun came over again after school because we said we would carve pumpkins together. Arjun carved an alien face with three eyes like Blip from my comic. I carved a pumpkin with a rocket on it. It was hard to do the fins because they kept breaking off. We scooped out all the guts and it was slimy. Arjun said it feels like the slime from Christmas. I saved the seeds and Mom roasted them. I want to plant some to see if they grow. Then we put candles in, and Arjun's alien looked so cool in the dark. It was spooky.
entries.highlight: Carved pumpkins with Arjun, who made one look like the alien from his comic, and saved the seeds to plant.

entries.title: Mars with Olympus Mons
entries.body: I drew a picture of Mars again. My first Mars was last New Year's Eve and it was just a red circle with me waving on it. This time I put Olympus Mons, the biggest volcano in the whole solar system. It is three times as tall as Mount Everest. I also drew the two little moons, Phobos and Deimos, which look like potatoes. I put a rover in the corner with its tracks behind it. Mom compared the two Mars pictures and said you can see how much I learned. I said the first one is still nice. It just did not have facts.
entries.highlight: Drew Mars with Olympus Mons and its potato-shaped moons, and compared it to his much simpler drawing from last year.

entries.title: Lights for my jetpack
entries.body: I needed supplies for my jetpack so me and Mom went to the hardware store. I want lights in the bottom of it so it glows like real rocket fire. I made a list. Battery pack, a string of tiny orange lights, and more duct tape because the last tape did not hold. The man at the hardware store showed me how the battery pack has a little switch. When we got home I put the lights inside the bottles. When I pressed the switch it glowed orange through the streamers. Dad said it is a circuit, the electricity goes in a loop. I am so ready for Friday.
entries.favorite: The lights glowing when I pressed the switch
entries.highlight: Bought a battery pack and lights at the hardware store with Mom and wired glowing rocket fire into his jetpack.

entries.title: Astronaut with a glowing jetpack
entries.body: Halloween! I was an astronaut with my cardboard jetpack and the orange lights inside. Arjun was an alien with glowing antennas and Ivy was a little pumpkin. My jetpack fell off twice. The first time was on the third house and the duct tape strap ripped. Dad fixed it with more duct tape. The second time it fell in a pile of leaves and the lights were still blinking in there. People said cool jetpack a lot. I got so much candy. When we got home I sorted it into a chart by type in my notebook. Chocolate won by a lot.
entries.favorite: My jetpack glowing in the dark
entries.highlight: Trick-or-treated as an astronaut with a glowing homemade jetpack that fell off twice, then charted his candy.

entries.title: Ice cream and the first cold night
entries.body: We went to the ice cream shop with my whole family, and it was the first really cold night. Dad said here we go again, ice cream in the cold. I got mint chip. Ivy tried to read the flavor names on the board. She can read some letters now. She said M is for mint like Luke. I helped her sound out vanilla. Then she ordered it herself and said please and thank you to the man. Last year she just pointed. On the way home I looked up and saw Orion coming up over the houses. Winter stars are coming back.
entries.highlight: Got ice cream with the family on the first cold night, helped Ivy sound out flavors, and spotted Orion rising.

entries.title: The rubber band piston
entries.body: I built version three of my space food machine. Back in August I changed the plans to roll the food in a tortilla so there are no crumbs. The hard part was the piston. A cardboard tube is too weak, so I made a new piston with a pencil and two rubber bands that snap it forward when you pull it back and let go. It pushes the cheese onto the tortilla. Then you turn the handle and the conveyor belt rolls it up. The first two tortillas fell off the side. The third one actually rolled! It looked like a messy burrito. Mom ate it and said it tasted like a regular quesadilla, but cold. That counts.
entries.favorite: The tortilla rolling up for real
entries.highlight: Built a third version of his space food machine with a rubber band piston that finally rolled up a tortilla.

entries.title: The woolly bear test
entries.body: I looked at bugs in the backyard and found a woolly bear caterpillar crawling across the patio. It is black on the ends and brown in the middle. Dad said some people say if the brown part is big, winter will be easy, and if it is small, winter will be hard. This one had a big brown part. But I said that is not real science, it is only one caterpillar. You would need to check at least a hundred caterpillars and compare it to a hundred winters. Dad laughed and said fair point. I wrote down the prediction anyway so I can check it in March. I let it go in the leaf pile.
entries.highlight: Found a woolly bear caterpillar and questioned the folk tale that it predicts winter, saying one caterpillar is not enough data.

entries.title: Betelgeuse is a red giant
entries.body: Dad and me looked at the stars from the backyard. It was cold so I wore my hat with the pom pom. Orion is all the way up now. I found his belt, three stars in a line, by myself. Then Dad showed me the reddish star at his shoulder. It is called Betelgeuse. It is a red giant, which means it is a really old star that puffed up huge. Someday it will explode in a supernova. Dad said not in our lifetime probably. I hope it does, because it would be so bright you could see it in the daytime. I wonder if it already exploded and the light just has not gotten here yet. I drew Orion in my moon journal even though it is not the moon.
entries.favorite: Seeing the red star in Orion's shoulder
entries.highlight: Found Orion's belt on his own and learned that Betelgeuse is an old red giant star that will someday explode.

entries.title: The lab moves back inside
entries.body: The garage got too cold for my lab, my fingers were freezing and my water froze in a cup. So I moved the lab back into my closet. It is crowded now because I have more stuff than last winter. I have the specimen shelf, the cicada shell, the moon journal, my lab notebook number two, and my green ribbon. This time I made a little corner for Ivy with her goggles and her picture cards. Last winter my sign said only scientists. I made a new sign. It says LUKE AND IVY'S LAB, SCIENTISTS AND ASSISTANTS ONLY. Ivy taped it up crooked but I left it.
entries.highlight: Moved his lab back into the closet for winter and made a new sign that includes Ivy as his assistant.

entries.title: School on the space station
entries.body: Tonight I thought about what school would be like on the space station. You would see sixteen sunrises a day, so maybe there could be sixteen recesses. Everybody would float, so you could do tag in three directions, up, down and sideways. Your pencil would float away unless you velcro it. Lunch would be tortillas, no bread, I know that from my book. And you would have to exercise for two hours every day so your bones stay strong. That is basically PE all day. I think Mr. Brooks would be good at teaching in space because he is so tall he could reach the ceiling.
entries.highlight: Imagined a school on the space station with sixteen sunrises, floating tag and tortilla lunches.

entries.title: Venus would be the worst school
entries.body: Today I thought about what school would be like on Venus. It would be the worst school ever. Venus is the hottest planet, even hotter than Mercury, because its thick clouds trap the heat like a blanket. It is hot enough to melt lead. And the clouds rain acid! Also, a day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus. It spins so slow. So one school day would last longer than a whole school year. I told Ivy that and she said then you would never get to go home. That is right. Venus school is a no. I would pick Mars or the moon.
entries.favorite: Telling Ivy a day is longer than a year
entries.highlight: Explained why a school on Venus would be terrible, including its acid clouds and a day longer than its year.

entries.title: Egg drop challenge planning
entries.body: Mr. Brooks announced an egg drop challenge for the whole third grade. In two weeks we drop our eggs off the top of the bleachers. I did an egg drop last December with Mom and the first one cracked and then the parachute worked. So tonight me and Mom tested some ideas. We wrapped an egg in bubble wrap and dropped it from the stairs and it was fine. But the rule is you can only use paper, straws, tape and one plastic bag. No bubble wrap. So I have to think of something else. I am thinking straws in a triangle cage, because triangles are strong. I learned that from the paper bridge with Felix.
entries.highlight: Started planning for the third grade egg drop challenge with Mom and thought of a triangle straw cage based on an earlier bridge experiment.

entries.title: Redrawing page one
entries.body: I redrew page one of my Captain Crater comic. The old page one is from last January and Captain Crater looks like a potato with arms. Now I know how to draw hands and helmets better. I also fixed the science. In the old one the moon had blue sky and now I made it black, because the moon has no air to make the sky blue. I put the old page and the new page next to each other and Mom took a picture. I am going to redraw every page so the whole comic is the same. That is going to take forever, but I want it to be good.
entries.favorite: Seeing the old and new page side by side
entries.highlight: Redrew the first page of his comic, fixing both the art and the science, and decided to redo every page.

entries.title: Movie day with Wes after Thanksgiving
entries.body: It was the day after Thanksgiving so there was no school. Wes's mom drove us to see the new animated movie. In the car Wes ate a turkey sandwich from his leftovers and kept poking me with the other hand. Annoying but funny. The movie was about a girl who builds a rocket in her backyard. Her rocket blew up the first time and she almost quit. Then she fixed it. Wes said that is like you. I said what? He said you always try again. I did not say anything but that made me feel good. We got popcorn and shared it.
entries.favorite: Wes saying I always try again
entries.highlight: Went to a movie with Wes the day after Thanksgiving, and Wes said the persistent rocket-building heroine was like him.

entries.title: Tidy-Bot's sock ramp
entries.body: Tonight I built the first real part of Tidy-Bot. It is not a whole robot yet, just a sock sorter. It is a ramp made from a cereal box, and at the bottom there is a little cardboard flap. If you put a sock in, it slides down the ramp into the laundry basket. If you put a Lego in, it is heavier and it bounces over the flap and into the toy bin. It only works about half the time. Dad said that is a great start, because engineers test things over and over. I tested it twenty times and wrote the results in my notebook. Eleven worked.
entries.favorite: My sock sliding into the right bin
entries.highlight: Built a cardboard sock-sorting ramp as the first real piece of his Tidy-Bot and tested it twenty times.

entries.title: Hot chocolate instead of ice cream
entries.body: We went to the ice cream shop with my whole family, but it was so cold that for the first time ever I did not get ice cream. I got hot chocolate with whipped cream. Dad said finally, I win. Ivy got a tiny ice cream in a cup anyway because she said she is not cold. She was shivering. Then Mom asked me why hot chocolate gets a skin on top when it cools down. I said I do not know, but I want to find out. I wonder if it has to do with the milk. I am going to put it on my question list in my notebook, which has fourteen questions now.
entries.highlight: Chose hot chocolate over ice cream for the first time on a cold family outing and added a new question to his notebook list.

entries.title: A rainbow from an old CD
entries.body: I made a rainbow in a different way. Dad found an old CD in the junk drawer. I shined my flashlight on the shiny side in my dark closet lab and a rainbow came out on the wall. It is not refraction like the glass of water, Dad said. It is called diffraction. The CD has tiny lines on it, so tiny you cannot see them, and they split the light. I tried my red flashlight and it only made red. That makes sense because there is only red in it to begin with. So a rainbow needs all the colors already inside white light. I wrote refraction and diffraction in my notebook next to each other.
entries.favorite: The rainbow stripes on my wall
entries.highlight: Made a rainbow with an old CD and a flashlight and learned the difference between refraction and diffraction.

entries.title: Saturn's rings got skinny
entries.body: I drew Saturn but it is different from my October drawing. We looked at Saturn in Big Blue last week and the rings looked really skinny, almost like a line. In July they looked bigger. I thought they were disappearing! Dad looked it up. Saturn is tilted, and as it goes around the sun, sometimes we see the rings from the side, edge on. So they look super thin. They are still there. I drew three Saturns in a row, one tilted a lot, one a little, and one edge on, and I drew Earth looking at them with arrows. I think that explains it.
entries.favorite: Figuring out the rings are tilted
entries.highlight: Noticed Saturn's rings looked thin in his telescope and drew a diagram showing how the planet's tilt changes our view.

entries.title: Shopping for the egg drop rules
entries.body: I needed supplies for the egg drop challenge so me and Mom went to the store. I made a list like a real scientist, but this time only with allowed things. Paper, straws, tape, and one plastic grocery bag. I picked the bendy straws because I can bend them into a triangle easier. I also got a dozen eggs so I can test a lot. Mom said a dozen is a lot of practice eggs, and I said scientists need a big sample size. She looked surprised I knew that. I learned it from Mr. Brooks. The cashier asked if we were baking and I said we are dropping.
entries.highlight: Shopped for egg drop materials within the challenge rules and explained to Mom why he needed many test eggs.

entries.title: Planet tag in the gym
entries.body: It was raining so we had indoor recess in the gym. We played planet tag, the game I made up in October. In the gym you have to orbit around the basketball hoop instead of the slide. There is a new rule now that Hazel invented. If you are Pluto you can come back if somebody shouts you are still a planet to us. Everybody shouts it all the time so Pluto never stays out long. Some first graders were watching and said can we join? I said yes and explained the rules slow. Mr. Brooks said the game keeps getting bigger every time.
entries.highlight: Played his planet tag game in the gym during indoor recess and explained the rules to first graders who asked to join.

entries.title: Ivy was not scared this time
entries.body: We watched the second wizard movie tonight. Last time Ivy hid under the blanket for the snake part, but this time she watched the whole thing. She said I am four and a half, I am brave. She even said the floating spell correctly, not wingardium lemonade. We all clapped. I explained again that real potions are chemical reactions and Ivy said I know, Luke, you told me a hundred times. Mom laughed. I made popcorn this time with Dad. He showed me how the kernels pop because there is water inside that turns into steam and bursts. Every single thing is science.
entries.highlight: Watched a wizard movie where Ivy was brave enough to watch the scary part, and learned from Dad why popcorn pops.

entries.title: Testing egg cages with Arjun
entries.body: Arjun came over to work on our egg drop designs together, but we each built our own. Mine is a triangle cage of bendy straws with the egg hanging in the middle by tape, so it does not touch the sides. Arjun made a paper parachute and a paper cup for the egg. We tested them off the top of the stairs. Both survived. Then we went higher, off the deck. Mine survived. Arjun's survived too but it was slower because the parachute opened. We tried to figure out whose was better. Arjun said the parachute slows it and I said the cage protects it. Maybe both together is best but we decided not to copy each other.
entries.highlight: Tested egg drop designs with Arjun from the stairs and the deck and debated whether a cage or a parachute was better.

entries.title: My egg survived the bleachers
entries.body: Today was the egg drop challenge. The whole third grade went out to the bleachers and Mr. Brooks dropped every egg from the very top. When it was my turn I could not breathe. My triangle straw cage hit the ground and bounced one time. I ran over and unwrapped the tape and the egg was perfect. Not even one crack. Mr. Brooks held it up and said look at this. Exactly one year ago I did my first egg drop with Mom and my first egg cracked and was all gooey. This time it worked the first try because I tested it a lot first. I am keeping the cage in my lab.
entries.favorite: Opening the cage and the egg was fine
entries.highlight: His straw cage egg survived the third grade bleacher drop on the first try, a year after his first egg cracked.

entries.title: Helping Arjun figure out what went wrong
entries.body: Arjun's egg cracked in the egg drop. His parachute got tangled and did not open, so it fell straight down. He was really sad and he did not want to talk at lunch. After school I asked if he wanted to figure out what went wrong, like the judge at the science fair did with me. We drew his parachute and I think the strings were too long so they tangled. Arjun said maybe he should have folded it differently. Then he said next year he is going to win. I said maybe we should be partners next year and do a cage with a parachute. Arjun said lab partners forever.
entries.highlight: Comforted Arjun after his egg cracked in the challenge and helped him figure out why his parachute failed.

entries.title: Mars school, take two
entries.body: I thought about school on Mars again. Last January I said recess would be longer because the Mars day is longer. That was right. It is called a sol and it is twenty four hours and thirty seven minutes. So it is only thirty seven minutes longer. That is not that much more recess, but I would take it. Now I also know the gravity on Mars is only about a third of Earth's. So you could jump almost three times higher. Basketball would be so easy. But dust storms can cover the whole planet for weeks. So there would be a lot of indoor recess, like today when it was raining.
entries.favorite: Jumping three times higher on Mars
entries.highlight: Revisited his idea of a school on Mars with exact facts about its day length and lower gravity.

entries.title: Snow ice cream
entries.body: It snowed for the first time this winter, a lot! So instead of going to the ice cream shop we made snow ice cream. You get clean fresh snow from the top of the table outside, and mix it with milk and sugar and a little vanilla. Ivy and I collected the snow in a big bowl. Dad said only from the top layer and no yellow snow, and Ivy laughed for five minutes. It tasted like a slushy. Then I looked at snowflakes on my black mitten with my magnifying glass. They all had six sides. Every single one. I wonder why it is always six.
entries.favorite: Making snow ice cream with Ivy
entries.highlight: Made snow ice cream with Ivy during the first snow of winter and noticed every snowflake had six sides.

entries.title: My Christmas list has one robot
entries.body: I wrote my Christmas list today. Last year I wanted a telescope and I got Big Blue. This year number one is a microscope, so I can look at snowflakes and bugs really close. Number two is a robot kit with a real motor so I can make Tidy-Bot move. The sock ramp only works about half the time and it does not move by itself, which is kind of the whole point of a robot. Number three is a new lab notebook because mine is almost full. Ivy dictated her list to me because she cannot write yet. Her number one was a puppy, which is not happening.
entries.favorite: Writing my list in neat letters
entries.highlight: Wrote a Christmas list asking for a microscope and a robot kit, and wrote down Ivy's list for her too.

entries.title: A microscope for Christmas
entries.body: Christmas! I got a real microscope! It has three lenses, a little light on the bottom, and glass slides. It is white and I named it Little Blue, because Big Blue is for stars and Little Blue is for tiny things. The first thing I looked at was salt, and every salt grain is a perfect little cube! Then I looked at my hair and it looked like a rope. Ivy wanted to look at her hair too so I helped her focus it. I also got a robot motor kit from Mom and Dad and a new lab notebook. Ivy got a stuffed puppy, not a real one. Best Christmas since Big Blue.
entries.favorite: Seeing the salt crystals are cubes
entries.highlight: Got a microscope for Christmas, named it Little Blue, and discovered under it that salt grains are tiny cubes.

entries.title: Public library microscope books
entries.body: There is no school because it is winter break, so Mom took me and Ivy to the big public library downtown. I wanted books about microscopes and I found three. One shows pond water under a microscope and there are tiny creatures swimming in it that you cannot see with your eyes. One is all about snowflakes, and it says they always have six sides because of how water molecules hold hands when they freeze. That answers my question from the snow day! Ivy got a book about a puppy, of course. The library card lady said I can take out ten books at a time. Ten!
entries.highlight: Visited the public library over winter break and found a book that answered his question about why snowflakes have six sides.

entries.title: Ice cream and the year in review
entries.body: We went to the ice cream shop with my whole family during winter break. I got mint chip in a cup and Dad got a hot coffee. While we ate Mom asked everyone what the best part of this year was. I could not pick one. Saturn's rings in July, my moon journal, the egg drop, teaching Ivy the cabbage water. Ivy said hers was being my lab assistant. Dad said his was the Father's Day crystal I made him. I think this year I did more real science than last year. Last year I mostly mixed things. This year I made predictions and tested them.
entries.favorite: Remembering all the things I did
entries.highlight: Reflected over ice cream on his favorite science moments of the year and noticed he did more real testing than the year before.

entries.title: Jupiter and four little moons
entries.body: Dad and me looked at the stars from the backyard and Jupiter was so bright, the brightest thing in the sky except the moon. We pointed Big Blue at it and I saw four tiny dots in a line next to Jupiter. Dad said those are its four biggest moons. Galileo found them four hundred years ago with a telescope that was not even as good as mine. One of them must be Io, the volcano moon I drew last January. I drew the dots in my moon journal. My plan is to look again tomorrow to see if they moved. If they move, that proves they are going around Jupiter.
entries.favorite: Seeing the four moons in a line
entries.highlight: Saw Jupiter's four largest moons through his telescope and planned to check whether they move to prove they orbit Jupiter.

entries.title: Science fair plan: hot, room, cold
entries.body: The science fair is in February. Last year my salt crystals were tiny and I got honorable mention. This year I am doing crystals again, but a real experiment with one thing changing. I wonder if temperature changes how big the crystals grow. So me and Mom went to the store for three jars, a big bag of salt, string and a thermometer. One jar goes in the fridge, one on the counter, one by the heater. My hypothesis is that the cold jar will grow the biggest crystals, because slow growing makes bigger crystals, I read that in my library book. Mom said this is a real science fair project.
entries.highlight: Planned a science fair experiment testing how temperature affects salt crystal growth, with a hypothesis based on his reading.

entries.title: A balloon in the freezer
entries.body: I did an experiment with a balloon instead of a balloon rocket. I blew up two balloons the same size and measured them with a string. Then I put one in the freezer for an hour. When I took it out it was smaller and wrinkly. Then I put it by the heater and it got big again! Mom said the air inside gets smaller when it is cold because the tiny bits of air slow down and squish together. That is why my soccer ball goes flat in the winter. I wrote it in my new lab notebook. It is the first experiment in notebook number three. I also checked Jupiter's moons last night and they moved!
entries.favorite: The balloon shrinking in the freezer
entries.highlight: Showed that a balloon shrinks in the freezer and grows by the heater, and confirmed Jupiter's moons had moved.

entries.title: Salt crystals under Little Blue
entries.body: I took one of the crystals from my science fair jars and put it under my microscope. The crystals are made of cubes stacked on cubes, like stairs going into the middle. Mom said it is called a hopper crystal. It looked like a pyramid upside down. The cold jar crystals are a little bigger so far, and the heater jar ones are lots of tiny ones crowded together. That matches my hypothesis. I measured them with a ruler and wrote it in a data table. Dad said I should take pictures through the microscope for my poster. We held the phone up to the eyepiece and it worked.
entries.highlight: Looked at his science fair crystals under the microscope, saw stair-step hopper crystals, and recorded early data that matched his hypothesis.

entries.title: Snowflakes and sledding with Wes
entries.body: It snowed again and Wes came over on Saturday. First we went sledding on the hill behind the school. Wes went down headfirst and got snow in his whole face. Then we came back and did experiments. I put black paper in the freezer so it was cold, then we caught snowflakes on it outside and looked with my magnifying glass before they melted. Wes caught one that was perfect, like the ones in pictures. Every one had six sides. I told Wes it is because of how the water molecules hold hands. He said that is weird but cool. We drank hot chocolate and it got a skin on top again.
entries.favorite: Wes's snowflake on the black paper
entries.highlight: Went sledding with Wes and then caught and examined six-sided snowflakes on frozen black paper.

entries.title: The giant moon rocket rolls out
entries.body: We watched a video of the giant moon rocket rolling out to the launch pad. It rides on a huge crawler machine that goes less than one mile an hour. It is slower than a turtle! It took almost the whole day to go four miles. Dad said this rocket is going to take astronauts around the moon, the first time people have gone to the moon since before he was born. I am going to watch the launch when it happens. I asked Dad why it needs to be so big and he said it takes a lot of fuel to get all the way to the moon. The moon is so far away. I wonder what the astronauts will see out the window when they go around the back side.
entries.favorite: The rocket moving slower than a turtle
entries.highlight: Watched the giant moon rocket roll slowly to its launch pad and learned it will carry astronauts around the moon.

entries.title: My first robot that moves by itself
entries.body: I built my first robot that moves by itself! I used the motor kit from Christmas. It is called a bristlebot. You take a toothbrush head and put a tiny buzzing motor and a battery on top. When you turn it on it shakes and the bristles make it walk forward. It went across the kitchen table and almost fell off the edge. Ivy chased it. It is not Tidy-Bot yet, it cannot pick up socks, but it moves by itself, which the sock ramp could not do. I named it Tidy-Bot Junior. My next idea is to put two motors so it can turn. Dad said I am becoming an engineer.
entries.favorite: The bristlebot spinning on the table
entries.highlight: Built his first self-moving robot, a toothbrush bristlebot powered by a motor from his Christmas kit.

entries.title: Twelve pages redrawn
entries.body: I redrew pages ten, eleven and twelve of my comic. That means twelve out of twenty pages are redrawn. These are the pages where the meteor hits the moon lab and the air starts leaking. I made the meteor hit with no flames this time, because there is no air on the moon to burn it up. I learned that last year but I forgot to fix it. I also drew the air leaking out as little swirls. Mr. Brooks said the drawings show movement, which is hard to do. I am trying to finish the whole thing by summer. It is my longest project ever.
entries.favorite: Drawing the meteor hitting the moon lab
entries.highlight: Redrew three more pages of his comic, correcting the science of meteors on the moon, and set a goal to finish by summer.

entries.title: Ice skating with Hazel
entries.body: Hazel's mom drove us to the ice skating rink on Sunday. In the car we played the science alphabet game and we got through the whole thing without getting stuck, even Q and X. Hazel's mom said she was impressed and she does not even know what quartz is. I had never ice skated before. I fell down like eight times. Hazel is really good and she pulled me around holding my hands. I asked her why ice is slippery and she said there is a tiny layer of water on top. We are going to look that up to be sure. By the end I could go a little by myself. My knees are so sore.
entries.favorite: Hazel pulling me around the rink
entries.highlight: Went ice skating for the first time with Hazel, fell many times, and wondered why ice is slippery.

entries.title: A motor on the conveyor belt
entries.body: I put a motor on my space food machine. Before, you had to turn the handle to move the conveyor belt. Now I took the extra motor from my Christmas kit and attached it with a rubber band, like a belt on a bike. When I turn the switch the belt moves by itself! It goes slow but that is good because the tortilla does not fly off. The rubber band piston still pushes the cheese on. So now it is half automatic. It is version four. I made Ivy a cheese tortilla roll and she said it tasted like the space station. She has never been to the space station.
entries.highlight: Added a motor to his space food machine so the conveyor belt moves on its own, making version four half automatic.

entries.title: Ice cream after Ivy's preschool show
entries.body: Ivy had a winter show at her preschool and we all went. She sang a song about snowmen and she was the loudest one. She waved at us in the middle of the song. After, we went to the ice cream shop with my whole family to celebrate her. Ivy got to pick first and she got bubblegum flavor. I got mint chip. She said Luke, did you see me? and I said you were the best snowman singer. She gave me a hug with sticky hands. I remember when she was three and she just cried at everything. Now she sings in front of people. I think I am proud of her.
entries.highlight: Went to Ivy's preschool winter show and celebrated her with family ice cream, feeling proud of how she has grown.

entries.title: Day twenty eight of the crystal jars
entries.body: I finished collecting data for my science fair project. It has been twenty eight days. The fridge jar grew the biggest crystals, almost one centimeter. The counter jar crystals are medium. The heater jar has tons of tiny crystals all crowded together and a crust on the side. So my hypothesis was right. Slow and cold makes bigger crystals. But I also found something I did not expect. The heater jar dried out the fastest, because the water evaporated faster. I am putting that on my poster under a part called surprises. Mr. Brooks says surprises are the best part of science.
entries.highlight: Finished collecting his science fair data, confirmed his hypothesis about cold and crystal size, and added an unexpected finding about evaporation.

entries.title: A book about geodes
entries.body: It was library day and I got a book about rocks and crystals for my science fair research. There is a page about geodes, which are rocks that look boring outside but when you break them open they are full of crystals inside. My book says some take millions of years to grow. That makes my crystals look really fast. It says the best crystals grow slowly in the ground where it is cool. That matches my experiment! I am going to put a fact about geodes on my poster. The librarian, Mrs. Hollis, said she remembered me from second grade and that I still ask the most questions.
entries.favorite: Learning geodes take millions of years
entries.highlight: Read about geodes for his science fair research and found that slow, cool growth matches his own crystal results.

entries.title: Snow tag and a first grader
entries.body: At recess there was still snow on the field so we played tag in the snow. It was really slow because everybody kept slipping. A first grader with a big puffy coat kept watching us and not asking. I remembered when I was too shy to ask and Arjun said just ask. So I went over and said do you want to join? He said yes really quietly. I let him be it first because that is the fun part. He tagged Hazel and screamed happily. His name is Toby. Now he waves at me every morning. The game kept getting bigger and we had like fifteen kids.
entries.favorite: Letting the little kid be it
entries.highlight: Invited a shy first grader to join snowy recess tag, remembering when he was once too shy to ask himself.

entries.title: What a moon base would need
entries.body: Today I made a list of everything a moon base would need. That is what I want to build someday, my lab on the moon. Number one is air, because there is none. Number two is water. My book says there might be ice in the dark craters at the moon's south pole, so the base should go there. Number three is protection from space rocks, since the moon has no air to burn them up. I wonder if the base should be underground. Number four is food, and I already invented the space food machine. Number five is a lab, of course. Number six, a place for Ivy. She would be my moon lab assistant.
entries.favorite: Thinking of the water ice at the south pole
entries.highlight: Made a list of what a moon base would need, choosing the south pole for its water ice and including his space food machine.

entries.title: Practicing my poster at the ice cream shop
entries.body: We went to the ice cream shop with my whole family and I practiced my science fair talk at the table, because the fair is on Friday. I pretended Dad was a judge. I explained my question, my hypothesis, my three jars, and my results. Dad asked what I would do differently, and I said I would use more jars at each temperature so it is a fairer test. Then Ivy asked why salt is salty. Nobody knew. That was the hardest question. Mom said judges might ask things I do not know, and it is okay to say I do not know but here is how I would find out. I am still nervous, but less than last year.
entries.highlight: Practiced his science fair presentation for the family over ice cream, with Dad playing a judge.

entries.title: The moon rocket has to wait
entries.body: We were watching the news about the giant moon rocket, and they said the launch is delayed because they found a leak in the fuel. I was really disappointed because I wanted to watch it this month. Then Dad said remember the launch that got scrubbed last May because of the wind? I said yes, I was so mad. He said and what did you learn? I said it is better to wait than to have something go wrong. Especially with astronauts inside. They are going around the moon and back, so it has to be perfect. So I am going to be patient. Patience is still hard, but I am better at it now. I put a note in my moon journal to keep checking.
entries.highlight: Was disappointed the moon rocket launch was delayed for a fuel leak, but remembered an earlier scrub and decided to be patient.

entries.title: Tag the day before the fair
entries.body: Tomorrow is the science fair and I was so nervous all morning that I could not focus during math. At recess Arjun said come on, tag will help. We played planet tag and I was the sun for a while. I chased everybody around the slide and by the end of recess I forgot I was nervous. I think running makes your brain calm down. Mr. Brooks said that is actually true, exercise helps with stress. Toby the first grader joined again and he is fast now. He tagged me twice. After recess I went through my poster one more time in my head and I felt ready.
entries.highlight: Played planet tag the day before the science fair and found that running helped calm his nerves.

entries.title: Blue ribbon for my crystal experiment
entries.body: Science fair today! My project was growing salt crystals at three temperatures. Last year my crystals were tiny and I almost cried. This year I had a hypothesis, three jars, data tables, microscope pictures, and a section called surprises. The judge asked why the cold jar made bigger crystals and I explained that slow growing lets the cubes stack up neatly. Then she asked something I did not know, and I said I do not know but here is how I would test it. I got a blue ribbon! Before the judging, a second grader named Poppy was crying because her volcano would not fizz. I told her to add way more baking soda, like me and Felix learned. It worked. She got honorable mention, just like me last year.
entries.highlight: Won a blue ribbon at the science fair for his crystal temperature experiment and helped a younger student fix her volcano.

entries.title: Ivy's very own egg drop
entries.body: Ivy wanted to do an egg drop like mine, so I helped her, but I made her do the thinking. I asked what she thinks would keep an egg safe. She said a pillow. I said we do not have a tiny pillow, so what is soft like a pillow? She picked cotton balls and a sock. She stuffed the egg in a sock full of cotton balls and taped it up. We dropped it off the stairs, and it survived! Then the deck. It survived again! Ivy did a dance. I did not tell her the answer at all, she figured it out. That is how Mrs. Patel and Mr. Brooks teach me. My blue ribbon is now on my lab door next to my green one.
entries.favorite: Ivy's egg surviving her own design
entries.highlight: Guided Ivy through designing her own egg drop with a cotton-stuffed sock that survived, letting her do the thinking.

entries.title: Lighting a bulb with foil
entries.body: Today in science we learned about circuits. Mr. Brooks gave each pair a battery, a little bulb and a strip of aluminum foil. Hazel was my partner. We had to figure out how to make the bulb light with only those three things. It took us ten minutes. The foil has to go from the bottom of the battery to the side of the bulb, and the bulb's bottom has to touch the top of the battery. It makes a loop and the electricity goes all the way around. When it lit up Hazel screamed. I said it is like my Halloween jetpack, that was a circuit too. Now I think I know why my lemon battery only flickered. The lemons were not strong enough to push much electricity.
entries.favorite: The bulb lighting when I touched the bottom
entries.highlight: Figured out how to light a bulb with only a battery and foil with Hazel, and connected it to why his lemon battery only flickered.

entries.title: A self watering moon garden
entries.body: I invented a machine that waters plants by itself, for my moon base garden. On my moon base list, food was number four, and food needs plants, and plants need water, but astronauts are busy. So I put a cup of water up high and ran a cotton string from the cup into the pot of soil. The water climbs along the string and drips into the soil slowly. It is called a wick. I did not believe it would work, because water going uphill seems impossible, but after one day the dry soil was wet! Mom said it is called capillary action. I planted a bean in the pot. Last year Hazel's beans grew toward the window, so I am going to see if mine does too.
entries.highlight: Invented a self-watering moon garden using a cotton wick and learned about capillary action.

entries.title: The syringe sauce pump
entries.body: I added a sauce pump to my space food machine. It is version five now. Dad got me two big plastic syringes from the pharmacy, the kind with no needle, and a plastic tube. You fill one syringe with sauce and connect it with the tube to the other syringe. When you push one, the other one pushes out. Dad said it is called hydraulics and real machines like dump trucks and excavators use it. So now the piston is not rubber bands anymore, it is hydraulic. It squirts ketchup right onto the tortilla before the conveyor belt rolls it up. The first time it squirted all over the wall. After four tries it went exactly in the middle. Mom said please only practice with water from now on.
entries.favorite: Squirting sauce exactly on the tortilla
entries.highlight: Added a hydraulic syringe sauce pump to his space food machine and learned how hydraulics work.

entries.title: Planetarium trip with Felix
entries.body: On Saturday Felix's family took me to the planetarium in the city. In the car we played the science alphabet game, and Felix tried to use planetarium for P before we even got there. At the planetarium you lie back in a big chair and the whole ceiling turns into the night sky with no city lights. There were so many stars I could not even find the Big Dipper at first because there were too many. Then the man pointed out Orion, and I knew Betelgeuse before he said it. He asked if anyone knew which star was red, and I raised my hand. Felix said Luke knows everything about stars. I said not everything. I still do not know what is inside a black hole.
entries.favorite: Lying back and seeing the whole sky
entries.highlight: Visited the planetarium with Felix's family and correctly named Betelgeuse when the presenter asked.

entries.title: My first experiment I planned and bought myself
entries.body: Today I planned an experiment all by myself and bought the stuff with my own allowance. I saved six dollars. I wrote the plan in my notebook first. The question is, which melts ice fastest, salt, sugar or sand? Me and Mom went to the store, but she waited by the front with Ivy and let me find everything and pay. I found the salt, and the sugar, and the sand was in the garden section. I had to ask an employee where it was. That was a little scary, but he was nice. It cost five dollars and twelve cents, and I got the change myself. When I came back Mom said you did that like a grown-up scientist. My prediction is salt, because of the ice cream in a bag.
entries.highlight: Planned his own experiment and bought all the supplies with his allowance, asking a store employee for help by himself.

entries.title: Pi Day with Felix
entries.body: It was Pi Day, three fourteen, so Felix came over and we did experiments with circles. Mr. Brooks told us about pi on Friday. If you measure around any circle and divide it by how wide it is, you always get a little more than three. We measured a plate, a cup, the lid of a jar, and a frisbee with a string and a ruler. Every single time it came out close to three. Felix said that is so weird, why is it always three? I said I do not know, it is just how circles are. Then Mom made a real apple pie and we measured that too before we ate it. Three point one. Then we ate it. That was the best part of the experiment.
entries.highlight: Celebrated Pi Day with Felix by measuring circles around the house and discovering the ratio was always a little over three.

entries.title: Checking the woolly bear prediction
entries.body: I looked for bugs for the first time this spring. Under the old log there were roly polies again, like every year. This time I put one under Little Blue for a few seconds on a damp paper towel. Its legs look like tiny shrimp legs. Mom said that is because roly polies are actually related to shrimp and crabs, not insects! Then I checked my woolly bear prediction from November. The caterpillar had a big brown stripe, which supposedly means an easy winter. But we had three big snows and lots of indoor recess. So the caterpillar was wrong. I wrote in my notebook, one caterpillar is not good data, which is what I said before. I let the roly poly go back under the log.
entries.favorite: The roly poly under the microscope
entries.highlight: Examined a roly poly under his microscope, learned they are related to shrimp, and found the woolly bear winter prediction was wrong.

entries.title: Reading my first lab notebook
entries.body: I was cleaning my lab and I found my first lab notebook from last January, the green one that says LUKE'S LAB NOTES. I read the whole thing. It was so funny. My handwriting was huge, and I spelled hypothesis wrong three different ways. One time I wrote hypothesee. My first prediction was that a long balloon would go farther than a round one. And I wrote, it made a big mess, on almost every page. Now I am on notebook number three and I have data tables and drawings with labels. I did not know I changed that much. I put the green notebook on my specimen shelf, because it is kind of a specimen too. A specimen of baby Luke science.
entries.highlight: Reread his first lab notebook from a year earlier and noticed how much his handwriting, spelling and methods had grown.

entries.title: A sundial on the equinox
entries.body: Today was the spring equinox, which means day and night are almost the same length everywhere on Earth. So I invented a sundial clock in the backyard. I put a stick straight up in the dirt, and every hour I put a rock at the end of the shadow and wrote the time on it with chalk. At nine o'clock the shadow was really long and pointed one way. At noon it was the shortest. By three it pointed the other way. Dad said the shadow moves because the Earth is spinning, not because the sun is moving. That is like the giant pendulum at the science museum. I knew it was spinning, but now I can see it with a stick. The rocks make a fan shape.
entries.highlight: Built a sundial from a stick and rocks on the spring equinox and saw the shadow move as the Earth turned.

entries.title: Bowling for Arjun's birthday
entries.body: On Saturday Mom drove me and Hazel to Arjun's birthday party at the bowling alley. Arjun is nine now, and I am still eight until September, which he keeps reminding me about. In the car Hazel and I argued about whether bowling is a sport or a science. At bowling I used the light ball, and it kept going into the gutter. Then I tried the heavy ball and it went straighter. I think heavier things are harder to push off course. That is called momentum, I think. In the fourth game I got my first strike ever. All ten pins. I jumped so high. Arjun's cake was a bowling pin. I gave him a pack of glow sticks and a card that said lab partners forever, nine years old edition.
entries.highlight: Went to Arjun's bowling birthday party, got his first strike, and noticed the heavier ball rolled straighter.

entries.title: How astronauts practice floating
entries.body: We watched a video about how astronauts train for space. They practice in a giant swimming pool with a model of the space station underwater, because floating in water feels kind of like floating in space. They wear their whole space suits in the pool. Some of them practice for six hours at a time. They also ride in an airplane that goes up and down really fast so everyone floats for a few seconds. I wonder if you could do a whole science experiment in those few seconds. The nickname is the vomit comet, which Ivy thought was the funniest thing. I asked Dad if I could practice floating at the pool this summer. He said yes, but no vomit comet. I think being an astronaut is more practice than I thought, like science fair times a thousand.
entries.highlight: Watched a video about astronaut training in underwater pools and parabolic flights and realized how much practice it takes.

entries.title: A clay moon base in art
entries.body: Today in art we learned something new. We used air dry clay to make sculptures, and we could make anything. I made my moon base from my list in February. The base part is gray clay with craters pressed in with a pencil eraser, like the foam moon I made with Dad. The dome is half of a ping pong ball, which Ms. Green let me bring. It was hard at first because the clay kept cracking when it dried, but she showed me to add a little water and smooth it. I made a tiny garden inside with green clay, and a little robot, which is Bolts, and a tiny Ivy in goggles. Ms. Green said I put a lot of thinking into it. It has to dry for a week.
entries.favorite: Making the dome out of a ping pong ball
entries.highlight: Sculpted his planned moon base out of clay in art class, complete with a dome, a garden and tiny versions of his characters.

entries.title: Volcano versus elephant toothpaste
entries.body: Ivy wanted to do a volcano, so we did two experiments to compare. The volcano was baking soda and vinegar. The elephant toothpaste was the one I bought supplies for last spring and never got to do. Mom did the hydrogen peroxide part because that is still grown-up only, and Ivy mixed the yeast with warm water. When we poured it in, the foam shot up out of the bottle like a giant toothpaste tube and it was warm. The volcano foam was cold. I asked Ivy why she thinks one is warm, and she said because the elephant is alive. I explained the yeast makes the reaction go fast and gives off heat. She said okay but I still think it is the elephant. I wrote both results in my notebook.
entries.highlight: Compared a baking soda volcano with elephant toothpaste alongside Ivy and noticed the toothpaste foam was warm.

entries.title: A planet show for movie night
entries.body: For movie night I picked a show about the planets instead of a regular movie. Ivy complained at first, but then she liked the part with the volcanoes on Io. I said I drew that one when I was seven. During the part about Saturn, I paused it and told everyone that Saturn would float in a bathtub. Dad said you told us that already, and I said I know, it is still cool. At the end, Ivy said all eight planets in order without any help. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. She learned them from the model over my bed. Then she said and Pluto, still a planet to us. That is from our planet tag rule. We all laughed. Mom made popcorn.
entries.highlight: Watched a planets documentary for movie night and Ivy named all eight planets in order without help.

entries.title: Tidy-Bot Junior learns to turn
entries.body: After movie night I worked on Tidy-Bot Junior. In January it could only walk forward, so I added a second motor on the other side. Now if only the left motor buzzes it turns right, and if only the right motor buzzes it turns left. It is like how a tank turns. I made the base bigger with a piece of cardboard and two toothbrush heads. I tested it on my bedroom floor. It drove straight into my pile of socks and got stuck, which to be fair is kind of what it is supposed to do. It just does not pick them up yet. Dad said maybe a scoop on the front. I sketched a scoop in my notebook. I think Tidy-Bot is going to take me years.
entries.favorite: Tidy-Bot Junior crashing into the sock pile
entries.highlight: Added a second motor so his bristlebot robot can turn, then sketched a scoop to help it pick up socks.

entries.title: Black hole tag
entries.body: At recess we tried a new version of planet tag. Arjun had the idea. One person is a black hole, and when you get tagged, you hold hands with the black hole and become part of it. So the black hole keeps getting bigger and bigger, like how real black holes get bigger when they eat stuff. By the end it was a chain of like twelve kids, and only Hazel was left running. She got pulled in at the very end. Everybody fell down laughing. I said in a real black hole you would turn into spaghetti, and somebody yelled spaghetti chain! So now that is the name of the end. Mr. Brooks watched and said he is glad we are not really spaghetti.
entries.favorite: Pulling Hazel into the black hole
entries.highlight: Played a new black hole version of tag where tagged kids joined a growing chain, inspired by how black holes grow.

entries.title: The deep ocean is like space
entries.body: It was library day and Mrs. Hollis said she had an April Fools book for me, but it was not a joke. It was a book about the deep ocean. I said I only read space books, and she said read it, it is like space. She was right. The bottom of the ocean is completely dark and freezing and the pressure would crush you, so people need special submarines, like a spaceship. There is a creature called an anglerfish with a light on its head to catch food. More people have walked on the moon than have been to the deepest part of the ocean. That surprised me the most. I read half of it already. Now I want a lab on the moon and one under the ocean.
entries.highlight: Read a book about the deep ocean that the librarian recommended and was surprised how similar it is to space.

entries.title: Being the tag referee
entries.body: Arjun hurt his ankle at soccer so he could not run at recess. He was sad sitting on the bench, so I sat with him for a while. Then we got an idea. We became the referees of tag. Every time somebody said I tagged you and the other person said no you did not, we decided. It was harder than I thought, because both of them were sure they were right. I said we need evidence, like in science. If anyone saw it, they are a witness. Arjun laughed and said you made tag into a science fair. One time I had to say my own friend Hazel was out, and she was mad for a second. But then she said okay, that is fair. Arjun and I are going to be referees until his ankle is better.
entries.favorite: Everyone agreeing my call was fair
entries.highlight: Sat with Arjun after he hurt his ankle and the two became fair-minded referees for the recess tag game.

entries.title: Roly polies choose the damp side
entries.body: There was no school this week for spring break, so I did a real bug experiment. I made a choice chamber out of a shoe box. One side has a damp paper towel and the other side has a dry paper towel. I put ten roly polies in the middle and waited ten minutes. My hypothesis was they would go to the damp side, because they always hide under the wet log. After ten minutes, eight were on the damp side and two were on the dry side. I did it two more times so it would be fair, and it was almost the same every time. So roly polies like damp places. My library book says it is because they breathe through gills, like the shrimp they are related to. I let them all go under the log again.
entries.favorite: Watching them all crawl to the wet side
entries.highlight: Built a choice chamber and found that roly polies prefer damp places, repeating the test three times to be fair.

entries.title: Nadia and the slime spot fossil
entries.body: Nadia came over on Saturday. We have not had a playdate in a long time because she is in the other class this year. We made slime for old times, but now we did it like scientists, measuring exactly how much glue and solution, because I know from my experiment last year the medium amount is best. It came out perfect the first time. Then Nadia found the slime spot by the couch from when we were seven. It is still there! Mom said it is a fossil now. We said we are still lab partners forever, even though now I have a lot of lab partners. Nadia said that is okay, she was the first one. That is true. She was.
entries.highlight: Made slime with Nadia again after a long time, measuring carefully this time, and found the old slime spot still on the carpet.

entries.title: Frog eggs at the nature center
entries.body: On Sunday Hazel came with us to the nature center. In the car, Hazel read the nature center map out loud and planned our whole route. At the nature center there is a pond with frog eggs in it. They look like clear jelly with black dots in the middle, and some of the dots were already wiggling. I wonder how they know when it is time to hatch. The ranger said they will be tadpoles in about a week, and frogs by the summer. She let us look at some pond water under a microscope, and there were tiny creatures swimming in it, like in my library book from Christmas break. Hazel said we should make a frog journal like my moon journal. I think that is a great idea. We are coming back in two weeks to check.
entries.highlight: Saw frog eggs and pond creatures at the nature center with Hazel, who suggested starting a frog journal together.

entries.title: School on Titan with wings
entries.body: Today I thought about what school would be like on Titan, which is Saturn's biggest moon. Titan is the only moon with thick air. And the gravity is really low. My book says that together means a person could flap big wings strapped to their arms and actually fly. So kids would fly to school! Recess would be flying tag. But Titan is so cold, around minus three hundred degrees, and it has lakes, but they are not water, they are liquid methane, which is like gas for a stove. So no swimming. And the sky is orange. I think Titan school would be the most fun but the most dangerous. You would need a heated suit and an air tank. A kid flying by would say can I join, and everybody would say yes.
entries.highlight: Imagined a school on Saturn's moon Titan, where low gravity and thick air would let kids fly, but methane lakes would make it dangerous.

entries.title: Car ride quiz for the Space Bee
entries.body: On the ride to school everybody quizzed me for the Space Bee. It is a quiz contest at school on Friday about space, and two kids from each third grade class get to be in it. Mr. Brooks picked me and Hazel. Wes read the questions off a list Mr. Brooks gave us. What planet has the most moons? I said Saturn, they keep finding more. What is the hottest planet? Venus, because the clouds trap heat. Then Wes made one up. What is Luke's favorite ice cream? Mint chip, everybody yelled. Wes kept poking me between questions. Annoying but funny. I got all of them right except one about the Kuiper belt. I did not know what it was. So that is what I am studying tonight.
entries.highlight: Got quizzed by friends on the ride to school for an upcoming school Space Bee and found one topic, the Kuiper belt, he still needed to study.

entries.title: Rocket stages for Ivy
entries.body: After dinner we watched a rocket launch on the computer. This time I could explain everything to Ivy. I told her rockets have stages. The first stage is the big bottom part, and when its fuel runs out, it falls away so the rocket is lighter. Then the second stage keeps going. That is called stage separation. When it happened on the screen, Ivy said there it goes! Then I stacked three paper cups and showed her. I held them up and dropped the bottom one, then the next. She wanted to do it like fifty times. I also studied the Kuiper belt. It is a ring of icy things past Neptune, and Pluto lives there. So Pluto has its own neighborhood, which is nice for Pluto.
entries.favorite: Ivy dropping the cups like stages
entries.highlight: Explained rocket stages to Ivy using stacked paper cups during a launch, then studied the Kuiper belt for the Space Bee.

entries.title: Second place at the Space Bee
entries.body: Today was the Space Bee in the gym and I got second place! The question I missed was what the closest star to Earth is. I said Proxima Centauri, but the answer was the sun, because the sun is a star. I knew that! I was so mad at myself for a minute. A fifth grader got first. Hazel got fourth. The best part was there was a Kuiper belt question and I got it right because I studied it on Tuesday. On the car ride home Felix's mom drove and Felix kept saying I would have said Proxima too. That made me feel better. He also yelled go Luke during the whole Space Bee, even when it was quiet. Mr. Brooks shushed him. Second place out of the whole school is still good.
entries.highlight: Placed second at the school Space Bee, missing a tricky question about the closest star, while Felix cheered loudly from the audience.

entries.title: The moon with real crater names
entries.body: I drew the moon, but this time I drew it exactly how it looks through Big Blue, using my moon map poster from my birthday. I labeled the real craters. Tycho has bright lines coming out from it in every direction, and that is just like the cocoa rays in my flour experiment last August. Copernicus is another big one. I also labeled the dark spots, which are called seas, even though there is no water in them, like Dad told me when I was seven. It took two whole hours. When I was little I drew the moon as a circle with a flag and footprints. This one looks like a map. I kept a little astronaut in the corner though, waving, because that is my thing.
entries.highlight: Drew a detailed moon map from his telescope view and labeled real craters such as Tycho and Copernicus.

entries.title: A menu for the space food machine
entries.body: Tonight I made a menu for my space food machine because now it can do three things: squirt sauce with the hydraulic pump, push food onto a tortilla with the piston, and roll it up on the motor conveyor belt. Menu item one is the space taco. Item two is the moon roll, which is peanut butter and banana. Item three is the Ivy special, which is just cheese, because that is all she eats. I thought about Earth Day next week, and how astronauts have trash problems. So version six will use edible wrappers made of rice paper. No trash at all. I put the menu on my lab wall. Felix wants to be a taste tester again, like when we did the crackers.
entries.highlight: Wrote a menu for his space food machine and planned edible rice paper wrappers so it would make no trash.

entries.title: Planning a weather station with Hazel
entries.body: On the ride to school everybody was singing and talking. Hazel and I made a plan for our next project as lab partners. We want to build a weather station for the backyard at her house. We will make a rain gauge out of a bottle, a wind vane from a straw and a paper arrow, and a thermometer in the shade. We will write the weather every day after school for a month, and see if we can predict tomorrow's weather. Hazel already wrote the plan in her notebook before the ride. She is really organized. Wes was listening from the back seat the whole time. He said he wants to be the weatherman who says it on TV. We said okay, he can read our data out loud.
entries.favorite: Hazel bringing the plan in her notebook
entries.highlight: Planned a backyard weather station project with Hazel during the ride to school, with Wes volunteering to be the weatherman.

entries.title: Heartbeats after tag
entries.body: Today in science we learned how to count our heartbeat by putting two fingers on our neck. Mr. Brooks had us count for fifteen seconds and multiply by four. Sitting down, mine was eighty beats a minute. Then at recess we played black hole tag really hard, and right after, I counted again. It was a hundred and twenty eight! My heart was going so fast. Then after we sat down for five minutes it went back to ninety. I told Mr. Brooks and he said that is a great experiment, you tested before and after. I asked why your heart goes faster, and he said your muscles need more oxygen when you run, so your heart pumps faster to bring it. So tag is science too.
entries.favorite: Counting a hundred and twenty beats
entries.highlight: Measured his heart rate before and after a hard game of tag and learned why exercise makes the heart beat faster.

entries.title: Tidy-Bot Junior picks up its first sock
entries.body: Tidy-Bot Junior picked up a sock! Well, sort of. I tried the scoop idea from March but socks are too floppy, they just slid off. So I remembered my magnet test from last August, and I got a strong magnet and taped it on the front of the robot. Then I clipped a paper clip on one of my socks.
