When Tidy-Bot Junior drove into it, the sock stuck on the magnet and it dragged it across the floor! Dad said that is cheating a little because you had to put paper clips on the socks. I said real inventors use whatever works. Dad said fair point. Now I need to figure out how to make it drop the sock in the basket. Maybe a lever. It is the closest Tidy-Bot has ever been to working.
entries.favorite: The sock coming up on the magnet
entries.highlight: Got his Tidy-Bot Junior robot to drag a sock using a magnet and a paper clip, the closest it has come to working.

entries.title: Captain Crater is finished
entries.body: I finished my comic book! Captain Crater and the Moon Lab is all done, twenty pages and a cover. I started it on January twenty fifth last year, so it took me more than a year. I redrew every page so they all match, and I fixed all the science mistakes, like the blue sky and the burning meteors. At the end Bolts saves the moon lab with the claw arm Captain Crater gave him, so it is a full circle ending like Mr. Brooks said. Dad made color copies at work and Mom helped me staple them. I made five copies. One for me, one for Ivy, one for Arjun, because he invented Blip, one for Mr. Brooks, and one for the school library. Mrs. Hollis said she would put it on the shelf.
entries.highlight: Finished his twenty-page comic book after more than a year of work and gave a copy to the school library.

entries.title: Meteors at four in the morning
entries.body: Dad woke me up at four in the morning to see a meteor shower. It is called the Eta Aquarids, and the meteors are tiny pieces of a famous comet. Dad said Earth goes through the comet's dust every year at this time. I wonder if the comet ever runs out of dust. We lay on a blanket in the backyard in our jackets. It was so quiet, only birds starting to wake up. For a long time we saw nothing and I almost fell asleep. Then one shot across the sky with a long tail! Then two more. Three total. Dad saw five because he did not close his eyes. I drew them in my moon journal. It was a school day, so I was really tired, but Mom said meteor showers are worth being tired for. I agree.
entries.highlight: Woke at four in the morning with Dad to watch the Eta Aquarid meteor shower and saw three meteors.

entries.title: Wes builds the wind vane
entries.body: Wes came over after school and we built the wind vane for the weather station, because Hazel said Wes could help if he did real work. We used a straw, a pencil with an eraser, a pin, and a paper arrow with a big tail. The tail has to be bigger than the point, or it does not turn the right way. We learned that because our first one pointed backwards. Then we used a compass to mark north, south, east and west on a paper plate underneath. When we took it outside the arrow pointed right into the wind. Wes did a weatherman voice and said today the wind is coming from the west, back to you Luke. He is actually really good at the voice. We are bringing it to Hazel's house on Saturday.
entries.favorite: The arrow pointing at the wind
entries.highlight: Built a working wind vane with Wes for the weather station and figured out why the tail needs to be bigger than the point.

entries.title: Shelving the space section
entries.body: It was library day, and Mrs. Hollis asked if I wanted to help her put the space books back in order. You have to put them in number order using the numbers on the spine. Space books are in the five hundreds. It is called the Dewey Decimal System. It was kind of like a puzzle. While I was shelving, I found my comic book on the shelf. It has a real library sticker on it now! Somebody already checked it out, a second grader. Mrs. Hollis said he loved Blip. I could not stop smiling for the rest of the day. I checked out a book about the Mars rovers, and I read half of it already.
entries.favorite: Finding my comic on the shelf
entries.highlight: Helped the librarian shelve space books and found his own comic book on the shelf, already checked out by a second grader.

entries.title: Hazel helps with Ivy's birthday present
entries.body: Ivy turned five yesterday, and Hazel came over today to help me finish my present for her. It is a star map for her bedroom ceiling. We took glow in the dark star stickers and put them on her ceiling in the real shapes of constellations. The Big Dipper, Orion, and Cassiopeia, which looks like a W. Hazel held the chart and told me where to put each one while I stood on the ladder, with Dad holding it. When we turned off the lights, it glowed. Ivy said whoa, and said it is like Big Blue but on my ceiling. I told her the Big Dipper was the first thing I ever found by myself. She said then it is the first thing I will find too.
entries.highlight: Made Ivy a glow-in-the-dark constellation ceiling for her fifth birthday with Hazel's help.

entries.title: Which wizard magic could be real
entries.body: We watched the last wizard movie tonight, so now we have seen all of them. During the movie I made a list in my head of which magic could actually be real someday. The invisibility cloak, Dad said scientists are working on special materials that bend light around things, so maybe. The moving staircases, those are just escalators that turn, so yes. The potions are chemistry, I already knew that. The flying broomsticks, no, but drones are kind of close. And talking portraits, that is just a video call. Ivy asked about the dragons, and I said no, sorry, but there are Komodo dragons. When I was seven I just wanted to make potions for real. Now I think a lot of magic is just science people have not figured out yet.
entries.favorite: Dad saying scientists are working on invisibility
entries.highlight: Finished the wizard movie series with his family and sorted which pieces of magic might become real science someday.

entries.title: Why brain freeze happens
entries.body: We went to the ice cream shop with my whole family on Sunday. I ate my mint chip too fast and got brain freeze, the kind that hurts behind your eyes. I asked why that happens, and nobody knew exactly, so Mom looked it up on her phone. The cold touches the roof of your mouth, and the blood vessels there get small really fast and then open back up, and your brain thinks it is a headache. The trick is to push your tongue on the roof of your mouth to warm it up. I tried it and it worked in like ten seconds! Then Ivy ate hers fast on purpose so she could try the trick. Mom said that is not how science works. Ivy said it is an experiment.
entries.favorite: Ivy getting brain freeze on purpose
entries.highlight: Got brain freeze from ice cream, learned why it happens, and Ivy gave herself one on purpose to test the cure.

entries.title: Graphing balloon rockets
entries.body: I did balloon rockets again but like a real scientist this time. I wanted to know if how many breaths you blow into the balloon changes how far it goes. I did two breaths, four breaths, six breaths and eight breaths, and I tested each one three times and measured with Dad's tape measure. Then I made a graph on graph paper, like Mr. Brooks showed us. The dots went up in almost a straight line, so more air goes farther. But eight breaths popped the balloon the second time. Mom asked why the balloon moves, and I said the air rushes out the back and pushes the balloon forward, for every action there is an opposite reaction. When I was seven I just said it zooms. Now I can say why it zooms.
entries.highlight: Tested how the amount of air affects balloon rocket distance, graphed the results, and explained the action-reaction force behind it.

entries.title: Saturn's rings are opening again
entries.body: I drew Saturn again for the next part of my tilted rings series. Last November the rings were almost edge on, like a skinny line. Dad found out that they are starting to tilt open again, a little more every year, and in a few years they will look wide again like in the pictures. So I drew a timeline. Last year's drawing with the line, this year's with the rings a tiny bit open, and then I drew what it will look like when I am thirteen, all the way open. I wrote the years under each one. Mom said it is like a growth chart for Saturn. I said Saturn is not growing, it is just tilting, and she said she knows, she was being funny.
entries.favorite: Drawing the rings a little wider
entries.highlight: Drew a timeline of Saturn's rings slowly tilting back into view over the coming years.

entries.title: My summer list, version two
entries.body: I made my summer experiment list for this year and I put it next to last year's list. Last year's list was five things and two said make a crater and Ivy's fizz. This year there are ten, and each one has a question and a hypothesis. Number one, does a solar oven get hot enough to cook s'mores? Number two, can I make an electromagnet? Number three, raise a monarch butterfly. Number four, make the lemon battery actually light up for real. Number five, see the Milky Way. Ivy has her own list now. She dictated it to me and then copied the letters herself. Her number one is make my own volcano without Luke helping. That is fair. I am going to let her.
entries.highlight: Wrote a ten-item summer science list with a question and hypothesis for each experiment, while Ivy made her own.

entries.title: The tadpoles have legs
entries.body: On Sunday we drove back to the nature center with Hazel to check on the frog eggs for our frog journal. In the car Hazel read me our notes from last time. She made me repeat the water temperature from April so I would remember it. At the pond, the eggs are gone, and now there are hundreds of tadpoles. Some of them are bigger and have two little back legs! The ranger said the front legs come next and then the tail gets absorbed back into the body. Hazel drew a tadpole with legs and I wrote the date and the water temperature, because we brought my thermometer. It is like the moon journal, but for frogs. We are going to come back once a month all summer to see them turn into frogs.
entries.favorite: Seeing a tadpole with back legs
entries.highlight: Returned to the nature center with Hazel and recorded tadpoles growing back legs in their shared frog journal.

entries.title: The rice paper taste test
entries.body: Felix came over to be the taste tester for the space food machine version six with the rice paper wrappers. You soak the rice paper in water for a few seconds and it gets soft and see-through. Then the hydraulic pump squirts sauce, the piston pushes the food on, and the conveyor belt rolls it up. The first one ripped. The second one was too wet and it stuck to the belt. The third one worked. Felix ate it and said it tastes like plastic but good. That is actually what rice paper tastes like. We gave the machine a score out of ten for each roll and wrote it in my notebook. The average was six. Felix said a real space food company would give it a seven.
entries.favorite: Felix saying it tastes like plastic but good
entries.highlight: Taste-tested rice paper wrappers from his space food machine with Felix and scored each attempt in his notebook.

entries.title: Issue two starring Ivy Star
entries.body: I started issue two of my comic. It is called Ivy Star and the Fizzing Planet, and this time Ivy Star is the main character, not Captain Crater. Ivy helped me write it. She told me the story and I wrote it down and drew it. In the story, Ivy Star discovers a planet where everything fizzes when you touch it, and she has to figure out why. I said she should use science, and Ivy said she would use her fizz power and also science. I said that is a good compromise. When Ivy was three, I did not even want her in my lab. Now she is the main character in my comic. She keeps asking to see each page. She says I have to draw her hair exactly right.
entries.highlight: Started a second comic book starring his sister's character, Ivy Star, and wrote the story with her.

entries.title: Third grade's future moon scientist
entries.body: Last day of school! Third grade is done. Mr. Brooks gave everybody an award at our class party. Mine said Future Moon Scientist, and under it it said, and still the best question asker. He remembered that Mrs. Patel gave me that award last year! Then he gave me a book about the moon missions and wrote in the front, for Luke, I cannot wait to read about your moon lab someday. I almost cried but I did not. I asked him one more question, which was whether he would come visit my moon lab. He said only if there is a space taco. This year I won a blue ribbon, made the egg survive, finished my comic, and got second in the Space Bee. Fourth grade is going to be hard to beat.
entries.favorite: Mr. Brooks saying I still ask the most questions
entries.highlight: Finished third grade and received Mr. Brooks's Future Moon Scientist award, along with a signed book about moon missions.

entries.title: Two graduations and two cones
entries.body: Ivy also finished preschool today, so after school we went to the ice cream shop with my whole family to celebrate both of us. Ivy called it her graduation. She wore a paper hat she made at school. Next year she is going to kindergarten at my school! She will be in the building with me. I told her where the library is and where Mrs. Hollis is and that she should ask Mrs. Hollis for the space books. She said she wants the puppy books. I got mint chip. She got rainbow sherbet and did not drop it. Dad said we have two big kids now. Then Mom took a picture of us with our cones and our awards. Ivy held my award upside down.
entries.highlight: Celebrated finishing third grade and Ivy finishing preschool with family ice cream, and told Ivy all about his school.

entries.title: A cereal box spectroscope
entries.body: I made a rainbow tool called a spectroscope. I found the instructions in the moon mission book from Mr. Brooks. You use a cereal box, a piece of an old CD, and a tiny slit cut in one end. When you look through it at a light, you see a rainbow inside the box. The cool part is different lights make different rainbows. The sunlight through the window was a smooth rainbow. But the kitchen light had stripes, only some colors with dark gaps between. The book says scientists use spectroscopes to figure out what stars are made of, from the colors of their light. So the rainbow is like a fingerprint. I remember when I was seven I made a rainbow in a glass and shook it into brown. Now I use rainbows to study stars.
entries.favorite: Seeing the stripes from the kitchen light
entries.highlight: Built a cereal box spectroscope and discovered different lights make different rainbow patterns, like fingerprints for stars.

entries.title: Growing a geode in an eggshell
entries.body: I grew a crystal geode in an eggshell. I read about geodes in February when I was researching the science fair. Real ones take millions of years but I did not want to wait that long. Mom bought alum from the spice aisle at the grocery store, which is a powder people use for pickles. We cleaned out half an eggshell, painted the inside with glue and sprinkled alum on it, and let it dry. Then we put it in a cup of hot water with a lot of alum and purple food coloring, and waited three days. Today I took it out and the inside was covered in purple sparkly crystals, just like the real geode pictures. It is the most beautiful thing in my lab. It goes on the specimen shelf right in the middle.
entries.highlight: Grew a purple alum crystal geode inside an eggshell, inspired by his science fair research on real geodes.

entries.title: Mars with a rover in Jezero crater
entries.body: I drew a picture of Mars, but this time not the whole planet, I drew what it would look like standing on it. I used my library book about the Mars rovers. The rover is in Jezero crater, which used to be a lake billions of years ago, so it is looking for signs of tiny life in the old mud. I drew the red rocks and the dusty pink sky, and the rover with its arm out drilling a rock. I put a tiny helicopter flying above it, because there really was one. In the corner I drew my astronaut waving, like always, standing next to the tracks. My first Mars drawing was just a red circle. Then Olympus Mons. Now I can draw it from the ground. Next I want to draw the sunset on Mars, which is blue.
entries.highlight: Drew a ground-level Mars scene with a rover in Jezero crater, his most detailed Mars drawing yet.

entries.title: A monarch caterpillar to raise
entries.body: Number three on my summer list is raise a monarch butterfly, and today I found a caterpillar on the milkweed plant in Mom's garden! It has yellow, black and white stripes and two little black antennas on each end. I put it in a mesh box with fresh milkweed leaves, because that is the only thing monarch caterpillars eat. It ate so much. My book says they get two thousand times bigger before they make a chrysalis. That is like if a baby grew to the size of a bus. I wonder if it can feel itself getting bigger. I am going to measure it every day with a ruler and write it in my notebook. Ivy named it Stripey. I said scientists do not name specimens and she said this one is not a specimen, it is a pet.
entries.highlight: Found a monarch caterpillar on the milkweed and started raising it, measuring it daily, while Ivy named it Stripey.

entries.title: Drawing the monarch life cycle
entries.body: In the evening I drew the whole monarch life cycle like a comic strip so I can check it off as Stripey grows. Box one is the tiny egg on a milkweed leaf. Box two is a caterpillar. Box three is the caterpillar hanging upside down in a J shape. Box four is the green chrysalis, which has gold dots on it, which seems fake but my book says it is real. Box five is the butterfly coming out with wet, crumpled wings. And box six is the butterfly flying away. Ivy wanted to help, so she colored the orange on the butterfly wings in box six. She went outside the lines a little but I said butterflies are not perfect either. I taped it to the side of the mesh box.
entries.highlight: Drew the monarch life cycle as a six-panel strip to track his caterpillar's growth, with Ivy coloring the wings.

entries.title: I saw the Milky Way
entries.body: We went camping in the mountains, really far from any city, and tonight I saw the Milky Way for the first time in my life. It was number five on my summer list. When it got all the way dark, there was a cloudy stripe going across the whole sky, but it was not clouds. It was millions of stars, so many and so far away that they blur together. Dad said that is our own galaxy, and we are inside it, looking at it from the side. I wonder if a kid on some planet far away is looking at our side of it right now. I could not stop looking. Back home we can only see maybe fifty stars. Here there were too many to count. I lay on the picnic table with Big Blue next to me and did not even use it. It was too big for a telescope. Ivy fell asleep in my lap.
entries.favorite: Seeing the Milky Way over the tent
entries.highlight: Saw the Milky Way for the first time on a family camping trip far from city lights, checking off a summer goal.

entries.title: School under the ice on Europa
entries.body: On the camping trip I thought about school on Jupiter again. When I was seven, I said Jupiter school would be a bad idea because there is no ground, and I said maybe Europa would be better. Now I know a lot more about Europa. It is one of Jupiter's moons, and it has a shell of ice on the outside, and under the ice there is a whole ocean of water, more water than on Earth. So my school would be under the ice, with big windows looking into the dark ocean, like the deep ocean book I read in April. Maybe there would be anglerfish type creatures. Scientists are actually looking for life there. Recess would be ice skating on the top, with Jupiter huge in the sky. Hazel would love that part.
entries.favorite: A school with windows to the ocean
entries.highlight: Imagined a school under Europa's icy shell overlooking its hidden ocean, building on an idea he had at age seven.

entries.title: A pizza box solar oven plan
entries.body: Number one on my summer list is the solar oven, so me and Mom went to the store for supplies. I already had a pizza box from Friday that Mom saved. I made a list. Aluminum foil, plastic wrap, black construction paper, tape, and graham crackers, marshmallows and chocolate for testing. The plan is, you cut a flap in the lid and cover it with foil to reflect the sunlight into the box. The plastic wrap makes a window that traps the heat inside, like a greenhouse, or like Venus! The black paper on the bottom soaks up the heat. My hypothesis is it will get hot enough to melt chocolate but maybe not cook the marshmallow. The cashier asked if I was going camping, and I said no, cooking with the sun.
entries.highlight: Gathered supplies with Mom for a pizza box solar oven and connected its heat-trapping design to the atmosphere of Venus.

entries.title: Solar oven s'mores on the hottest day
entries.body: Today was the hottest day of the year so far, so I tested the solar oven. I put my thermometer inside and pointed the foil flap at the sun. After thirty minutes the thermometer said one hundred and fifty five degrees inside the box! Outside it was ninety. I put a s'more inside, and after twenty minutes the chocolate was totally melted and the marshmallow was soft and puffy, but not toasted brown like a campfire. So my hypothesis was right, mostly. I gave the first one to Ivy because she waited the whole time with me, and the second one to me. I moved the box every twenty minutes to follow the sun, and that made it hotter. I wrote in my notebook, next version, a bigger flap.
entries.favorite: The chocolate melting in the sun
entries.highlight: Tested his solar oven on a hot day, measured it reaching 155 degrees, and made s'mores with melted chocolate.

entries.title: Ivy Star finds the fizz
entries.body: I drew pages three and four of the Ivy Star comic. In these pages, Ivy Star lands on the fizzing planet and every rock she touches fizzes. She takes a sample with her tiny tweezers and looks at it under her microscope, which looks exactly like Little Blue. She discovers the rocks are made of baking soda and the rain is vinegar. That was Ivy's idea! She said it should be the volcano stuff. I think that is a really smart idea for a five year old. I drew a big fizzing rock with bubbles going everywhere and Ivy laughed so hard at it. She asked if she can show it to her kindergarten teacher in August. I said yes, if we finish it by then. That means two pages a week.
entries.favorite: Ivy laughing at the fizzing rock
entries.highlight: Drew more pages of the Ivy Star comic based on Ivy's own idea that the fizzing planet is made of baking soda and vinegar rain.

entries.title: My biggest Jupiter ever
entries.body: I drew my biggest Jupiter ever on a giant poster paper Dad got me. My first Jupiter was in November when I was seven. Mom saved it in the drawer, so I took it out to compare. The first one was a circle with stripes and a red spot that was way too big. This one has the belts and zones with their real colors, the Great Red Spot the right size, and swirls in the clouds. I put the four big moons in a line, the way I saw them in Big Blue in January. Io is yellow with volcanoes, Europa is white with cracks, Ganymede is the biggest, and Callisto has the most craters. Mom said she is putting this one in a frame instead of on the fridge. That made me feel like a real artist.
entries.highlight: Drew a large detailed poster of Jupiter and its four big moons and compared it to his first Jupiter drawing from age seven.

entries.title: My own kayak on the lake
entries.body: On Saturday we drove to the lake near Grandma's and rented kayaks, and for the first time I got my own kayak instead of sitting with Dad. Mom and Ivy were in one and Dad was in another. At first I kept going in circles, because I paddled harder on one side. Dad said switch sides every stroke, left, right, left, right. Then I went straight! We paddled all the way to a little island in the middle of the lake. I remember the first time I went rafting last August, I held onto the rope the whole time and screamed. Today I paddled by myself and I was not scared at all, even when a boat went by and made waves. Ivy yelled you are so brave, Luke, from her kayak.
entries.favorite: Paddling all the way to the island
entries.highlight: Paddled his own kayak for the first time, figured out how to go straight, and reached an island without being scared.

entries.title: The soggy wrapper problem
entries.body: I have a problem with the space food machine. The rice paper wrappers get soggy after a few minutes and they tear before you can eat them. I tested it four times and timed them. They tear after about six minutes on average. So I thought about what real astronaut food does. Most of it is dried, freeze dried, so there is no water. When you want to eat it, you add water. So maybe my machine should do it backward, make the roll and then dry it with a fan so it stays crispy. Or keep the wrappers dry until the very last second. I drew both ideas in my notebook and wrote pros and cons for each one. Engineering is mostly solving problems you made by solving other problems.
entries.highlight: Timed how quickly his space food wrappers turned soggy and designed two possible fixes inspired by freeze-dried astronaut food.

entries.title: School on Pluto, finally
entries.body: I thought about what school would be like on Pluto, because I studied the Kuiper belt for the Space Bee and Pluto lives there. Pluto is so far away that the sun looks like a really bright star, so school would be dark all the time. It is around minus four hundred degrees. Pluto has a giant glacier shaped like a heart, and my book says it is made of frozen nitrogen. So the playground would be on the heart. And one year on Pluto is two hundred and forty eight Earth years, which is even worse than Neptune for birthdays. But Pluto has five moons, and its biggest moon is so big that they kind of orbit each other like a dance. I would name my school Still A Planet Elementary, from our tag rule.
entries.highlight: Imagined a dark, frozen school on Pluto's heart-shaped glacier and named it after a rule from his planet tag game.

entries.title: Fireflies one year later
entries.body: Last June I counted firefly flashes and guessed the fast ones were boys and the slow ones were girls, but I did not know. This year I did it better. I sat on the back steps with Mom's phone stopwatch and timed the flashes of the ones flying up high and the ones sitting in the grass. The flying ones flashed every five or six seconds in a J shape. The ones in the grass waited and then flashed back about two seconds later. I looked it up after, and it turns out the flying ones really are mostly males and the ones in the grass answering are mostly females! So my guess from last year was kind of right, but for a different reason. It is not fast or slow, it is flying versus answering. I wrote it in my notebook.
entries.favorite: Seeing the flash patterns are different
entries.highlight: Timed firefly flashes and discovered that flying males and grounded females signal in a call and answer pattern.

entries.title: A potion party for Ivy
entries.body: Tonight we had a wizard movie night, but first I set up a potion party for Ivy in the kitchen. I made a potion station with three cups of red cabbage water, which looks like purple potion. Then I gave her little cups of lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda water and soap water, and told her to guess what color each one would make before she poured. She wrote the guesses herself with her new five year old writing. Lemon turned pink, she guessed right. Baking soda turned green, she guessed blue, close. Mom and Dad tried too. Then we watched the movie with popcorn and Ivy had her potion cup next to her the whole time. Two years ago I wanted to make potions for real. Now I am teaching my sister how.
entries.highlight: Hosted a cabbage water potion party for Ivy before movie night where she wrote her own predictions for each color change.

entries.title: A moon phase wheel
entries.body: I drew a moon phase wheel. It has been almost a year since I started my moon journal, and I have three notebooks of moon drawings now. So I made something with all of it. I drew eight moons in a circle on a paper plate, new, crescent, quarter, gibbous, full, and back down. Then I put another paper plate on top with a window cut out, and a brass fastener in the middle so it spins. When you turn it, the window shows each phase one at a time. On the back I wrote the names and why it happens, the sun lights up different amounts of the moon as it goes around us. I made one for Ivy too so she can learn the moon like I did.
entries.highlight: Turned a year of moon journal observations into a spinning moon phase wheel and made a second one for Ivy.

entries.title: Ivy reads the flavor board
entries.body: We went to the ice cream shop with my whole family. And today Ivy read the whole flavor board by herself. Last November she was sounding out vanilla with me letter by letter. Today she read chocolate, strawberry, cookie dough, and even pistachio, which is a really hard word. The man behind the counter clapped. She got cookie dough, and she ordered it herself, and she paid with her own dollar. I got mint chip, of course, I have gotten mint chip every single time, I think about fifty times. Dad said maybe I should try something new. I tried a tiny taste of pistachio. It was good, but I still like mint chip better. Some experiments just confirm what you already know.
entries.favorite: Ivy reading cookie dough by herself
entries.highlight: Watched proudly as Ivy read the whole ice cream flavor board on her own, while he stuck with mint chip after tasting pistachio.

entries.title: A launch at science camp
entries.body: This week is science camp again. This year I am in the oldest group. Today our counselor, who is studying aerospace engineering in college, put a rocket launch on the big screen, and the whole group counted down. Afterward she told us she worked at a rocket company last summer as an intern and got to see a real launch in person. She said you feel the sound in your chest, not just hear it. I asked her a million questions, like how loud and how far away you stand and whether the ground shakes. She said I ask better questions than her college classmates. Then we built straw rockets that you launch by blowing into a tube. I changed the fins three times. My last one went across the whole gym.
entries.highlight: Watched a rocket launch at science camp with a counselor who had seen one in person, and asked her many questions.

entries.title: Drying the wrappers with a fan
entries.body: I tried the fan idea for the soggy wrapper problem. Dad gave me a little desk fan, and I set it up at the end of the conveyor belt so the roll gets blown on right after it is rolled. It worked better! The wrappers stayed together for fourteen minutes instead of six. But the sauce inside dried out too and got kind of crunchy, which is gross. So I tried the other idea too, keeping the wrapper dry until the last second and only squirting the sauce right before you eat it. That was the best one. Sixteen minutes and the sauce was still good. So the winner is idea two. I wrote both results in a chart. Version seven is going to have the sauce pump at the very end instead of the beginning.
entries.highlight: Tested both of his soggy wrapper fixes, measured how long each roll held together, and chose to move the sauce pump to the end.

entries.title: Real volcanoes are different shapes
entries.body: At science camp today we learned that real volcanoes come in different shapes, and we made models of two kinds with clay and baking soda. A shield volcano is wide and flat, like the ones in Hawaii, and the lava is runny so it spreads out far. A cone volcano is tall and steep, because the lava is thick and it piles up. Then we made the lava runny or thick by adding more or less dish soap and flour to the vinegar. The runny lava spread out over the whole tray, and the thick lava stayed close to the top. Olympus Mons on Mars is a shield volcano, which I told the whole group. When I was seven I thought volcanoes were just mountains that explode. Now I know why they are shaped the way they are.
entries.favorite: My shield volcano being so flat
entries.highlight: Built two types of volcano models at science camp and learned how runny versus thick lava shapes a volcano.

entries.title: The lemon battery finally lights up
entries.body: I finally made the lemon battery work for real! Last summer the tiny light only flickered. After the circuits unit with Mr. Brooks, I knew why. The lemons were not strong enough, and some of my wires were not touching the right metal. This time I used six lemons, and new zinc screws and copper strips from the hardware store, and I connected them in a line, copper to zinc, copper to zinc, so the push of each lemon adds up. I also used a tiny LED instead of a regular light, because LEDs need less electricity. When I touched the last wire, the red LED turned on and stayed on, not flickering at all. Mom and I yelled so loud Ivy came running. I measured it with Dad's meter. Almost five volts. From lemons!
entries.favorite: The light staying on and not just flickering
entries.highlight: Finally got his lemon battery to light an LED steadily, a year after it only flickered, by applying what he learned about circuits.

entries.title: Hardware store for an electromagnet
entries.body: Number two on my summer list is make an electromagnet, so me and Mom went to the hardware store. This time I went to the counter and asked the man myself. I said I need copper wire with the coating on it for an electromagnet, a big iron bolt and a battery holder. He asked if I wanted thin or thick wire. I did not know, so I asked which is better, and he said thinner wire lets you wrap more loops, and more loops means a stronger magnet. I did not know that. He gave me a whole roll of thin wire. When we left, Mom said I used to hide behind her at stores, and now I talk to everybody. I think it is because now I know what questions to ask.
entries.highlight: Asked the hardware store clerk on his own for electromagnet supplies and learned that more wire loops make a stronger magnet.

entries.title: School on an asteroid
entries.body: Today I thought about what school would be like on an asteroid. Some asteroids are only as big as a town. The gravity is so tiny that if you jumped, you might jump right off and float into space forever. So everyone would have to wear a rope tied to the school. Recess would be really slow tag where you bounce in slow motion and take a whole minute to come back down. Lunch would be tied down too. One cool thing is that some asteroids are full of metals, like iron and nickel, and even gold, so maybe the school could be built out of the asteroid itself. My moon base list said to protect from space rocks, but on an asteroid school, you would be the space rock. That is kind of funny.
entries.favorite: Jumping off the asteroid by accident
entries.highlight: Imagined a school on a tiny asteroid where low gravity would make kids tie themselves down to avoid floating away.

entries.title: My electromagnet can let go
entries.body: I built my electromagnet in the lab. I wrapped the thin copper wire around the iron bolt one hundred times, I counted, and connected the ends to the battery. It picked up eleven paper clips! Then I unhooked the battery, and they all dropped. And then I realized something. This solves my Tidy-Bot problem from April! Tidy-Bot Junior could drag a sock with a regular magnet, but it could not let go of the sock. An electromagnet can be turned off. So the robot can grab the paper clip sock, drive to the basket, turn the magnet off, and the sock drops in. I ran to tell Dad and I was talking so fast he made me say it twice. He said that is how real scrap yard cranes work.
entries.favorite: The paper clips dropping when I unhooked it
entries.highlight: Built an electromagnet that lifted eleven paper clips and realized it could let his Tidy-Bot robot finally drop socks into the basket.

entries.title: School on Mercury, hot and cold
entries.body: Today I thought about what school would be like on Mercury, the closest planet to the sun. You would think it would just be hot, but it is hot and cold. On the day side it is hot enough to melt metal, and on the night side it is colder than Antarctica, because Mercury has almost no air to hold the heat in like a blanket. And one day, from sunrise to the next sunrise, lasts about one hundred and seventy six Earth days. So you would have half a year of daytime and then half a year of night. The weirdest part is that there is ice on Mercury, in craters at the poles where the sun never shines. So my Mercury school would be in a crater at the pole, in the shade forever, with the ice for drinking water.
entries.favorite: The ice hiding in Mercury's craters
entries.highlight: Imagined a school on Mercury and figured out it would need to be in a shaded polar crater where ice hides from the sun.

entries.title: The spider who rebuilds every night
entries.body: I found a huge orb weaver spider web between the fence and Mom's tomato plants. It is a big wheel shape with a zigzag in the middle. I measured it with Dad's tape measure, and it was almost two feet across. Then I noticed something. In the morning the web is perfect and sparkly with dew, but by night it is broken from bugs and wind. And then the next morning it is perfect again. My library book says orb weavers eat their old web and spin a new one every night! I wonder how she knows the pattern without anybody teaching her. I did not believe it, so I set an alarm and checked at six in the morning, and she was finishing the last circles. I watched her for twenty minutes. I did not touch the web. I named her Charlotte because Ivy said I had to.
entries.favorite: Seeing the web sparkle with dew
entries.highlight: Measured an orb weaver spider's web and got up early to watch it rebuild the web, confirming what his library book said.

entries.title: A science kit for Ivy's kindergarten
entries.body: Ivy starts kindergarten in three weeks, at my school, so me and Mom went to the store to make her a science kit with my own allowance. I made a list. A little notebook with a puppy on it, crayons, a tiny ruler, and safety goggles in her size. At home I put everything in a pencil box. And then I decided to give her my old magnifying glass, the one I had when I was seven, that I used to look at the green beetle and the roly polies under the log. It has a scratch on it from when I dropped it on the patio. Ivy hugged it and said she will take care of it forever. I have Little Blue now anyway. I wrote IVY'S FIELD KIT on the box in my best letters.
entries.favorite: Giving Ivy my old magnifying glass
entries.highlight: Bought Ivy a kindergarten science kit with his own allowance and gave her his old magnifying glass.

entries.title: School on a comet
entries.body: Tonight I thought about what school would be like on a comet. Comets are like dirty snowballs, ice and dust and rock all mixed up, and they go around the sun in giant stretched out orbits. So for most of the year your school would be super far away and frozen. But when the comet gets close to the sun, the ice turns into gas and makes a huge glowing tail. The tail always points away from the sun, even when the comet is going away, because the sunlight pushes it. That surprised me. So the school would have a giant tail behind it, and you could see it from Earth. The meteors I saw with Dad in May were just leftover dust from a comet. So my comet school would make meteor showers for other kids to see.
entries.highlight: Imagined a school riding a comet and connected comet dust to the meteor shower he watched with Dad.

entries.title: Crickets are thermometers
entries.body: I found out that you can tell the temperature by counting cricket chirps. My bug book says to count how many times a cricket chirps in fourteen seconds, and then add forty, and that is the temperature in Fahrenheit. My prediction was that it would be way off. So tonight I sat on the back steps with Mom's phone stopwatch. I counted thirty eight chirps in fourteen seconds. Thirty eight plus forty is seventy eight. Then I ran inside and checked the thermometer on the porch, and it said seventy nine degrees! Only one degree off! I did it three more times and it was always close. The book says crickets chirp faster when it is warm because their bodies are cold blooded and speed up. I wonder if it works with other bugs too, like katydids. So crickets are basically thermometers with legs. I told everyone at dinner.
entries.favorite: My cricket math matching the real thermometer
entries.highlight: Tested a rule for estimating temperature from cricket chirps and found his calculation was within one degree.

entries.title: A switch for Tidy-Bot's magnet
entries.body: I needed parts for Tidy-Bot so me and Mom went to the hobby store that has an electronics section. Last week I figured out the electromagnet can let go of socks, but right now I have to unhook the wire with my hand, and that is not a robot, that is just me. I need a switch. The lady there helped me pick a push button switch, a red one, and a battery pack with four batteries for more power. She asked what I was building and I explained the whole Tidy-Bot story, from the crane arms to the sock ramp to the bristlebot. She said I should enter it in an invention contest. I said maybe when it works. I also got some wires with clips on the ends, so I do not have to twist them. That will save a lot of time.
entries.highlight: Shopped at a hobby store for a switch and battery pack so his Tidy-Bot's electromagnet can grab and release socks on command.

entries.title: Ivy's first rafting trip
entries.body: We went rafting on the river again, and this year Ivy was finally big enough to come, on the calmer part of the river. She was so nervous, she held onto the rope with both hands, exactly like I did my first time. So I sat next to her and said the bumpy parts are called rapids, and the water goes fast because the river gets narrow. That is what Hank the guide told me last summer. When we went through the first rapid, Ivy screamed and then started laughing, which is also exactly what I did. I held her hand. By the end she let go of the rope and tried to paddle. The guide this year let me sit in the front and yell paddle forward for everyone. Dad said I went from scared to captain.
entries.favorite: Holding Ivy's hand through the bumpy part
entries.highlight: Took Ivy on her first rafting trip and reassured her through the rapids, just as he had been reassured the summer before.

entries.title: Ivy's crystals and not telling her
entries.body: Ivy wanted to grow salt crystals all by herself, because her summer list said do my own experiment without Luke helping. So I only watched. She put hot water in a jar and stirred in salt, but only two spoons. I knew right away it was not enough to be saturated, because that is exactly what happened to me at my first science fair. I really, really wanted to tell her. But I did not. I remembered how the judge did not tell me the answer, she asked me why I thought it happened, and that is how I learned it forever. So I am going to wait. If her crystals are tiny, I will ask her why she thinks they are tiny. Mom saw me biting my lip and whispered that is real teaching.
entries.highlight: Watched Ivy make salt crystals with too little salt and chose not to correct her, so she could discover the mistake herself.

entries.title: Red flashlights for a meteor party
entries.body: Tonight is the Perseid meteor shower, the biggest one of the summer, so me and Mom went to the store for a meteor watch party. I made a list. Red cellophane, rubber bands, popcorn, and bug spray. I covered Ivy's flashlight and Mom's flashlight with red cellophane, so they glow red like my birthday flashlight. I explained to Ivy that your eyes take about twenty minutes to get used to the dark, and white light ruins it right away, but red light does not. She asked why, and I said I am not totally sure, it is something about the cells in your eyes. That is going on my question list. We are going to lie on the trampoline tonight. My prediction is I will see ten meteors. Ivy's prediction is one hundred.
entries.highlight: Prepared red-filtered flashlights for a family Perseid meteor shower party and explained night vision to Ivy.

entries.title: The frogs are real frogs now
entries.body: Hazel and I went back to the nature center for the last entry in our frog journal. In April they were jelly eggs with black dots, then in May they were tadpoles with back legs, and today they are tiny frogs, only as big as my thumbnail, hopping all around the edge of the pond. Some still had a little stub of a tail. One jumped right onto my shoe and Hazel screamed happily. We counted twenty three froglets in ten minutes. Hazel wrote the final page and I drew the whole life cycle with arrows from egg to frog. The ranger asked if she could make a copy of our journal to show other kids who visit. Hazel and I looked at each other and said yes at the same time. Lab partners forever, for real.
entries.highlight: Completed a months-long frog journal with Hazel by recording tiny froglets, and the ranger asked to copy it for visitors.

entries.title: Ivy raises her own monarch
entries.body: Stripey flew away in July after ten days in the chrysalis, and I let him go from the milkweed. Today Ivy found her own monarch caterpillar on the same plant, with her magnifying glass, the one I gave her! She wanted to raise it herself. I helped her set up the mesh box, and showed her how to put fresh milkweed in every day. Then she got out the tiny ruler from her field kit and measured it all by herself. She wrote the number in her puppy notebook, a two and a little line for the half. She named it Stripey Two. I told her that scientists usually use numbers instead of names. She said she knows, that is why it has a number in it. I think that is actually a clever answer.
entries.highlight: Helped Ivy set up a box to raise her own monarch caterpillar, which she found and measured herself with her field kit.

entries.title: Tidy-Bot drops its first sock
entries.body: Tidy-Bot dropped a sock into the basket! I have been working on Tidy-Bot since I was seven, when it was just a drawing with crane arms. Now it is Tidy-Bot Senior. It has two motors to drive and turn, the electromagnet on the front, and the red button switch. I clipped a paper clip on a sock, and drove Tidy-Bot into it with the switch on, and the sock stuck. Then I drove it to the laundry basket and pressed the button, and the magnet turned off and the sock fell right in. I screamed so loud Dad came running. We did it ten times and it worked seven. It does not make my bed. It does not see socks by itself. But it picks them up and puts them away, which was the whole idea. Mom said I still have to clean my room.
entries.favorite: Hearing the sock drop into the basket
entries.highlight: Got his Tidy-Bot robot to pick up a sock with an electromagnet and drop it in the laundry basket, more than a year after first drawing it.

entries.title: Ivy Star issue is finished
entries.body: I finished the Ivy Star comic, just in time for Ivy to bring it to kindergarten! It is twelve pages. At the end, Ivy Star figures out that the fizzing planet is made of baking soda and the rain is vinegar, and she uses that to make a giant fizzy volcano that launches her rocket home. Ivy wrote THE END herself, in her own letters, on the last page. My first comic took me more than a year. This one took less than three months, because I am faster at drawing now and I had a co-writer. Dad made copies again. Ivy is going to give one to her kindergarten teacher. She said she is going to tell everyone that her brother drew it and she wrote it. That is true. It was a good team.
entries.highlight: Finished the twelve-page Ivy Star comic in under three months with Ivy as co-writer, in time for her to share it at kindergarten.

entries.title: First day of fourth grade and kindergarten
entries.body: First day of school today, and it was a double first day. I am in fourth grade and Ivy is in kindergarten at my school! I walked her to her classroom holding her hand, and she showed her teacher the Ivy Star comic right away. Then I went to my classroom. My teacher is Ms. Alvarez. She has a real model of the solar system hanging over her desk, and a box of circuits on the shelf. She said this year we are going to learn about electricity and energy, and do a big research project about anything we want. I already know mine. It is going to be about how to build a base on the moon. Felix and Wes are both in my class this year. At pickup, Ivy ran out and said kindergarten is the best.
entries.highlight: Started fourth grade with Ms. Alvarez on the same day Ivy started kindergarten, and walked his sister to her classroom.

entries.title: Ivy counts down by herself
entries.body: After our first day of school we watched a rocket launch on the computer to celebrate. This time Ivy did the whole countdown by herself, from ten all the way to liftoff, and she did not skip seven, which she used to do. When the first stage dropped away she said stage separation! like I taught her with the paper cups in April. I almost could not believe it. I told her that in second grade I watched a rocket launch in Mrs. Patel's class and the whole class counted down. Maybe someday Ivy's class will do that too. She said she is going to ask her teacher tomorrow. Then she said when she grows up she wants to be the one who presses the launch button. I said I will be the astronaut and you can launch me.
entries.highlight: Watched a rocket launch after the first day of school as Ivy counted down on her own and correctly called out stage separation.

entries.title: Showing Ivy Saturn's rings
entries.body: Saturn is up in the evening again, so after dinner Dad and I set up Big Blue in the backyard. And tonight I showed Ivy Saturn's rings for the first time. I had to aim it myself, because Dad said I know how now. It took me a few tries to find it, and then I had to hold Ivy up so she could reach the eyepiece and tell her to close her other eye. She was quiet for a second and then said it looks like a sticker. That is exactly what I thought when I was seven, that it did not even look real. The rings are a little more open than last year, just like my timeline drawing said. Ivy said she wants to see it every night. I said only on clear nights, that is the rule.
entries.highlight: Aimed his telescope on his own to show Ivy Saturn's rings for the first time, and she reacted just as he had at seven.

entries.title: Jupiter for my all about me poster
entries.body: Ms. Alvarez gave us a homework assignment to make an all about me poster for the classroom wall. In the middle I drew Jupiter, because it was my first space drawing ever, back in second grade. Around it I drew all my favorite things. Big Blue the telescope, Little Blue the microscope, a mint chip ice cream cone, my lab door with the green ribbon and the blue ribbon, Tidy-Bot Senior holding a sock, Captain Crater, and Ivy in her goggles. I wrote facts on little stickers, like I have seen Saturn's rings, and I have kept a moon journal for one year. At the bottom I wrote, when I grow up I want a lab on the moon. It took the whole evening. Ivy said I forgot to put her puppy, but she does not have a puppy.
entries.favorite: Fitting all my favorite things on the poster
entries.highlight: Drew an all about me poster for fourth grade with Jupiter at the center, surrounded by his telescope, microscope, ribbons and inventions.

entries.title: One year of the moon journal
entries.body: It has been one year since I started my moon journal, on August twenty seventh last year, when there was no moon at all and I drew an empty circle. Now I have four notebooks of moon drawings. Tonight Dad and I looked at the moon, and it was almost full, really bright, and I drew it. Then I flipped through all the pages. The first drawings are kind of messy, just white shapes. By the end, I was labeling craters like Tycho and Copernicus, and writing the time and if it was cloudy. I counted, and I drew the moon two hundred and thirty one times. I missed some nights for clouds and for being sick. Dad said that is real dedication. I think I am going to keep going until I am ten. Maybe forever.
entries.highlight: Marked one year of his moon journal with two hundred thirty one drawings and noticed how much more detailed they had become.

entries.title: A crossover comic idea
entries.body: After I looked at the moon, I started planning issue three of my comic. It is going to be a crossover, which means two heroes from different comics meet each other. Captain Crater gets a distress signal from the fizzing planet, and he flies there and meets Ivy Star. At first they argue about whether to use science or fizz power, and then they figure out they need both. That is kind of like real life. Blip and Bolts are in it too. I asked Ivy if she wants to co-write again and she said yes, but only if Ivy Star gets to be the boss for half of it. I said that is fair. I made a plan with eight boxes, one for each part of the story, so I do not get stuck on the ending this time.
entries.highlight: Planned a crossover third comic bringing Captain Crater and Ivy Star together, outlining the ending first so he would not get stuck.

entries.title: Ivy found the Big Dipper by herself
entries.body: Tonight Dad and I took Ivy outside to look at the stars. I wanted to see if she could find the Big Dipper, because it is on her ceiling from the glow stickers we made for her birthday. I did not point. I said what Dad said to me when I was seven, try to find it, it looks like a pot with a handle. She looked for a long time, and she kept pointing at random stars. Then she yelled found it! And she was right. It was the Big Dipper. She found it by herself. I gave her a high five. When I found it, it was January and so cold my nose hurt. Tonight it was warm and the crickets were chirping. Dad said that is passing it on. Ivy said now she knows two things, the Big Dipper and Saturn.
entries.favorite: Ivy pointing and yelling found it
entries.highlight: Taught Ivy to find the Big Dipper the way Dad taught him, without pointing, and she found it on her own.

entries.title: Should we build a school on Mars?
entries.body: Ms. Alvarez gave us our first writing assignment, a persuasive essay, which means you pick a side and try to convince people with reasons. Mine is called Should We Build a School on Mars. My answer is not yet. Reason one, the gravity is only about a third of Earth's, and scientists do not know what that does to growing kids' bones. Reason two, dust storms can cover the whole planet for weeks. Reason three, there is no air you can breathe and the radiation is dangerous without thick walls. But I said someday yes, once there is a moon base first, because the moon is closer to practice on. When I was in second grade I just said recess would be longer. Ms. Alvarez read my essay to the class as an example of using evidence.
entries.favorite: Ms. Alvarez reading my essay to the class
entries.highlight: Wrote a persuasive essay arguing a school on Mars should wait, using evidence about gravity, dust storms and radiation, and his teacher shared it with the class.

entries.title: I bought Ivy's ice cream
entries.body: On Saturday we went to the ice cream shop with my whole family. This time I paid for Ivy's ice cream with my own allowance, because she had a hard first week of kindergarten. She cried on Wednesday because a kid took her crayon, and she said she did not want to go back. I told her that in second grade I was too shy to ask to play tag, and now I make up the tag games. She got bubblegum flavor and I got mint chip. She said thank you big brother, in a fancy voice. Then she told me she made a friend named Rosie and they played house at recess. I told her that is how it starts. First you make one friend, then everyone joins. Mom looked at Dad and smiled.
entries.highlight: Bought Ivy an ice cream with his allowance after her hard first week of kindergarten and encouraged her about making friends.

entries.title: Planning my birthday experiment stations
entries.body: My birthday party is on Saturday, so me and Mom went to the store to get supplies for experiment stations. I am planning everything myself this year. Station one is elephant toothpaste, and Mom will do the peroxide part, still. Station two is cabbage water potions, like Ivy's potion party. Station three is the electromagnet, to see who can pick up the most paper clips. Station four is straw rockets from science camp. I made a list of everything we needed for each one and checked it off at the store. Then at home I made instruction cards for each station with pictures, like the card I made for Ivy when she was four. Mom said I planned it like a real teacher. I said I planned it like a real scientist, which is basically the same.
entries.highlight: Planned and shopped for four experiment stations for his own ninth birthday party, writing instruction cards for each.

entries.title: Fourth grade tag starts small
entries.body: At recess in fourth grade there are new rules. We are not allowed on the little kid playground anymore, because that is for kindergarten and first grade, which is where Ivy is. So we play on the big field. Today it was just me and Felix at first, and we did regular tag, just the two of us, which is kind of boring with two people. Then Wes came over and asked to join, and then two kids from the other fourth grade class. By the end we had seven. I saw Ivy through the fence on the little playground playing with Rosie, and she waved at me. I waved back. Felix said we should try to get the whole grade to play one day. I said that would be the biggest game of tag ever.
entries.favorite: Felix saying the whole grade could play
entries.highlight: Started a recess tag game with Felix on the big fourth grade field that slowly grew to seven kids.

entries.title: The class Mars vote
entries.body: After Ms. Alvarez read my Mars essay, she had the class do a debate and then a vote. The question was, should people move to Mars in our lifetime. Half the class said yes because it would be an adventure, and half said no because it is too dangerous. Felix was on the yes side and I was on the not yet side. He said people used to think flying was too dangerous too. That was a really good point and I did not have an answer right away. Then I said flying was dangerous until we practiced a lot, and that is why we should practice on the moon first. In the end the yes side won by two votes. But Ms. Alvarez said three kids changed their minds because of my argument. Tomorrow I turn nine!
entries.favorite: Losing the vote but changing minds
entries.highlight: Debated whether people should move to Mars in a class vote, lost narrowly, but persuaded three classmates to change their minds.

entries.title: Nine years old and a moon cake
entries.body: It was my birthday! I am nine now. My cake looked like a planet, well, a moon. It was round and gray with craters pressed into the frosting, and Mom and I made it together, and I labeled Tycho with a tiny flag. I had a science party with Felix and five other kids, and all my experiment stations worked. The elephant toothpaste went the highest it ever has, and Felix won the electromagnet station with twenty two paper clips. Ivy was my station helper and wore her goggles the whole time. For presents I got a model rocket kit from Mom and Dad, a real one that launches with a little engine and comes down with a parachute. Dad said we will build it together next weekend. Best birthday ever, I think.
entries.highlight: Turned nine with a moon cake and a science party with Felix, and got a real model rocket kit to build with Dad.

entries.title: Building the model rocket with Dad
entries.body: On Saturday Dad and I built the model rocket from my birthday. It took the whole afternoon. The instructions had twenty two steps. The body is a cardboard tube, and the nose cone is plastic. The hardest part was the fins, because if they are even a little bit crooked, the rocket will spin and go sideways. So we made a paper guide to keep them exactly straight while the glue dried. I remember when I was seven, we made a paper towel tube rocket and Dad said fins keep a rocket straight. Now I know why. Saturn's rings on my ceiling model were the hardest part back then, and the fins were the hardest part today. Dad said every project has one hard part. Then we painted it white with a red nose. It is called Moon Lab One.
entries.highlight: Spent a Saturday building a real model rocket with Dad, carefully aligning the fins and naming it Moon Lab One.

entries.title: Moon Lab One launches
entries.body: Today after school Dad and I launched Moon Lab One at the big field by the middle school. Mom and Ivy came to watch. We set up the launch pad, which is a metal rod on a stand, and Dad connected the wires to the launch box. Ivy got to do the countdown, because she is the expert now. Ten, nine, eight. On zero I pressed the button and it went WHOOSH, so fast I almost missed it. It went up maybe three hundred feet, it was a tiny dot. Then the parachute popped out and it floated down slowly. We had to run across the whole field to get it. It landed in the grass and nothing broke. Ivy said can I press the button next time? I said yes, because she wants to be the launch person.
entries.highlight: Launched his model rocket with Dad as Ivy led the countdown, and it rose about three hundred feet before parachuting safely down.

entries.title: Ivy gets her own lab shelf
entries.body: I gave Ivy her own shelf in our lab today. She has so much stuff now. Her field kit, her puppy notebook, Stripey Two's empty chrysalis, and her crystals. Her first crystals from August were tiny, and when I asked her why she thought they were tiny, she said maybe it is the salt. I did not say anything else. I made her a label for the shelf, IVY'S RESEARCH. Then I made a new lab rules poster, because the old one from Nadia and me just said always wear goggles. The new one has five rules. Wear goggles. Write your prediction first. Grown-ups pour the dangerous stuff. Clean up the slime. And number five, a failed experiment still teaches you something. Ivy asked what that means. I said you will find out.
entries.highlight: Gave Ivy her own shelf in their lab and made a new five-rule poster ending with the lesson that failed experiments still teach.

entries.title: Drawing the harvest moon
entries.body: Last night was the full moon in September, which is called the harvest moon, because a long time ago farmers used its light to finish harvesting at night. It came up really orange and huge over the houses. I know it only looks huge because of the moon illusion, I learned that last October with Dad. But it still looked amazing. Today I drew it with chalk pastels, the way I learned in art in third grade. I blended orange and yellow and a little red for the moon, and black and dark blue for the sky, and I drew the roofs of our street as black shapes. In the corner, a tiny astronaut waving, my signature. Mom said this is the best one I have made with pastels. I think it is because I drew what I actually saw.
entries.favorite: The orange moon over the roofs
entries.highlight: Drew the orange harvest moon over his street in chalk pastels, applying what he knew about the moon illusion.

entries.title: Research for my moon base project
entries.body: It was library day, and I started research for my big fourth grade project on how to build a base on the moon. Mrs. Hollis helped me find two books and a website about real plans for moon bases. Scientists really want to build near the south pole, because of the ice in the dark craters, which is exactly what I said in my moon base list in February! Some plans use the moon dirt to 3D print the walls. That is so cool. I wonder if they would let a kid help design one. I took notes on index cards, one fact per card, like Ms. Alvarez showed us, and I wrote where each fact came from. Then during kindergarten library time I saw Ivy, and she was checking out a puppy book, of course. But she also had a book about the moon. She said for the moon journal she wants to start.
entries.favorite: Finding a real NASA moon base plan
entries.highlight: Started research for his fourth grade moon base project and learned real scientists also favor the moon's south pole, as he had predicted.

entries.title: Saturn at its brightest
entries.body: This week Saturn is the brightest it gets all year, because Earth is passing right between Saturn and the sun. Dad said it is called opposition. So tonight we set up Big Blue in the backyard and I found it fast. The rings are definitely more open than last November, when they looked like a line. And this time I noticed a little dot next to Saturn. Dad checked his app and said that is Titan, Saturn's biggest moon! The moon from my Titan school idea, where kids could fly with wings. I saw it with my own eyes. I drew Saturn and Titan in my moon journal, even though it is a moon journal for our moon. I think Titan counts. It is a moon. I want to see Saturn every year at opposition now.
entries.favorite: Seeing a moon next to Saturn
entries.highlight: Observed Saturn at opposition with its rings more open than the year before and spotted its moon Titan for the first time.

entries.title: Tidy-Bot's demonstration day
entries.body: I did a Tidy-Bot demonstration for my whole family in my room. I made tickets and Ivy handed them out. I put paper clips on five socks and threw them on the floor. Then I drove Tidy-Bot Senior with the controls, and it picked up each sock with the electromagnet and dropped it in the basket. It got four out of five. The fifth one, the paper clip fell off. Then I explained the whole history on a poster I made. Version one crane arms, version two wheels, version three bumpers, the sock ramp, the bristlebot, two motors, the regular magnet, and the electromagnet. Dad asked what is next, and I said making it find socks by itself, maybe with a camera. Mom said she is so proud, but I still have to make my bed.
entries.favorite: Tidy-Bot getting four out of five socks
entries.highlight: Gave his family a demonstration of Tidy-Bot Senior picking up socks and presented a poster of every version since age seven.

entries.title: Crossover comic, page six
entries.body: I drew pages five and six of the crossover comic with Ivy. In these pages, Captain Crater and Ivy Star argue about whether to fix the fizzing planet with science or with fizz power. Ivy wanted Ivy Star to say I am the boss now, so I drew a big speech bubble for her. Then Captain Crater says, but you need to test it first. And Ivy Star says, okay, but you need to try new things. I think that is actually what Ivy and I are like in real life. I like to test everything first, and she likes to just try it. Ms. Alvarez said she wants to read it when we finish. This time I planned the ending first, so I know how it ends. They both win. I am not telling anyone until it is done.
entries.highlight: Drew more pages of a crossover comic co-written with Ivy, where the two heroes argue in ways that mirror the real siblings.

entries.title: Ivy figured out the salt
entries.body: After school Ivy came running into the lab, because her second batch of salt crystals was done. This time she put in so much salt that some stayed at the bottom of the jar, all on her own. And the crystals were way bigger! I asked her, why do you think these ones are bigger? She said because the first time I did not put enough salt, so I did it more. Then she pointed at our lab rules poster and said, rule number five, the failed one taught me. I could not stop smiling. That was exactly what happened to me at my first science fair, and I did not tell her the answer at all. She figured it out herself. I told Mom and she said, you were a good teacher by not teaching. That is kind of confusing, but I understand it.
entries.favorite: Ivy saying the failed one taught me
entries.highlight: Saw Ivy figure out on her own that more salt makes bigger crystals, and she pointed to the lab rule that failed experiments still teach.

entries.title: Ice cream after the biggest tag game
entries.body: On Saturday we went to the ice cream shop with my whole family, and I told them all about the biggest game of tag ever again, because Dad missed the first time I told it. I told them how it was just me and Felix, and then everyone kept saying can I join, and Ms. Alvarez tagged Wes. Ivy said her recess has a tag game too, and she asked a kid if she could join, and they said yes. She said she was brave, like me. I got mint chip, of course. Ivy got bubblegum again, and she let me taste it this time, which she never does. Dad said that is the second big thing this week, the tag game and Ivy's crystals. I said science and tag, my two favorite things.
entries.favorite: Telling the whole tag story at the table
entries.highlight: Retold the story of his record-breaking tag game over family ice cream, and Ivy shared that she had bravely joined a tag game too.

entries.title: Twelve woolly bears is better data
entries.body: I found woolly bear caterpillars again in the backyard, and this time I did it the right way. Last November I said one caterpillar is not good data, and I was right, because it predicted an easy winter and we got three big snows. So this year I looked for a whole week, in our yard and the park and Hazel's yard. I found twelve woolly bears and measured the brown stripe on every single one with a ruler, and I wrote it in a table. Most of them had medium stripes. But here is the thing. Even twelve is not enough, and scientists say the stripe actually depends on how old the caterpillar is, not the weather. So I wrote my conclusion, the woolly bear is cute but it is not a weatherman. Hazel agreed.
entries.highlight: Collected data on twelve woolly bear caterpillars to test the winter-prediction folk tale and concluded it was not reliable.

entries.title: School on a spaceship to another star
entries.body: Today I thought about if school was on a spaceship going to another star. The closest star after the sun is Proxima Centauri. I remember because I said that answer at the Space Bee and got it wrong, because the closest star is the sun! Proxima is so far that even the fastest spaceship we have would take thousands of years to get there. So the kids who start on the ship would never arrive. Their great great great great grandkids would. So the school would have to teach everything, how to grow food, fix the ship, and history about Earth, which they would never see. That is kind of sad, but also really cool. I think the kids would love space but miss ice cream. I would bring mint chip seeds, if those existed.
entries.highlight: Imagined a school aboard a spaceship traveling thousands of years to Proxima Centauri and thought about kids who would never see Earth.

entries.title: Ivy joins the ride home
entries.body: Ivy rides home from school with us now on Tuesdays, because her kindergarten gets out at the same time. Today everybody was singing and talking, and Ivy sang the loudest, like at her preschool show. Wes kept poking me, like always, annoying but funny. But then he poked Ivy too, and I was about to tell him to stop, but Ivy poked him back and said annoying but funny! She has heard me say it a hundred times. Everybody laughed so hard. Then Wes taught Ivy the science alphabet game. For A she said astronaut, for B she said Big Dipper, and for C she said crystals. Wes said she is going to be smarter than me. I said that would be fine with me. She is already a good scientist. I just do not tell her too much.
entries.favorite: Wes teaching Ivy the alphabet game
entries.highlight: Rode home from school with Ivy, who poked Wes back with his own catchphrase and played the science alphabet game.

entries.title: Notebook number five
entries.body: I started lab notebook number five tonight. Before I wrote in it, I put all of them in a row on my desk. Number one is the green one from second grade, LUKE'S LAB NOTES, with the hypothesee spelling. Number two has the moon phases and the magnet test. Number three has the science fair crystals and the bristlebot. Number four has the lemon battery that finally worked and the electromagnet and Tidy-Bot. Number five is empty. On the first page I wrote a question list for this year. Can Tidy-Bot find socks by itself with a camera? What is inside a black hole, really? Why does red light not ruin your night vision? Why is salt salty, which was Ivy's question. I think I will be asking questions my whole life. That is fine, because that is the job.
entries.highlight: Lined up all five of his lab notebooks from second grade on and started the newest one with a fresh list of questions.

entries.title: My moon poem in reading
entries.body: Today in reading Ms. Alvarez taught us about poems that do not have to rhyme. We had to write one about something we see every day. I wrote about the moon, since I have drawn it more than two hundred times. My poem goes, Every night you change your face, a crescent, half, a gibbous shape, you never really change at all, the sun just lights you different. You keep the footprints like a secret. You have ice hiding in the dark. Someday I will build my lab on you. Ms. Alvarez asked me to read it out loud. I was a little nervous, but I did it. She said the part about the footprints like a secret was beautiful. Hazel said she liked the gibbous part, because nobody knows that word.
entries.favorite: Ms. Alvarez asking me to read it out loud
entries.highlight: Wrote a free verse poem about the moon in reading class that used his moon journal knowledge, and read it aloud to the class.

entries.title: Real spiders and fake webs
entries.body: Everybody on our street put up fake spider webs for Halloween. But I went to check on Charlotte, the real orb weaver from August, and her web was gone. I looked everywhere. Then I found a little tan ball stuck under the fence rail, fluffy like cotton. My bug book says it is an egg sac! Orb weavers lay their eggs in the fall, and the mom usually dies when it gets cold, but the babies hatch in the spring. That made me a little sad about Charlotte. But Ivy said it is okay, because now there will be hundreds of Charlottes. That is actually a good way to think about it. I marked the spot in my notebook so I can check in April. I wonder how many of the babies will stay in our yard. The fake webs are not as good as Charlotte's real one.
entries.highlight: Found the egg sac of the orb weaver spider he had watched in August and planned to check on it in spring.

entries.title: Jetpack two point zero stayed on
entries.body: Halloween! I was an astronaut again, but with jetpack two point zero. Last year my jetpack fell off twice, once at the third house and once in the leaves. So this year I engineered it. I used real backpack straps sewn on by Mom instead of duct tape, and I made the bottles lighter, and I put the battery pack in the middle so it was balanced. It did not fall off even once. The orange lights glowed all night. Ivy was the moon, with a gray costume and craters we painted together, and she said she was my mission. Felix was a mad scientist. People kept asking if my jetpack was real. After, I sorted my candy into a bar graph. Chocolate won again, by even more than last year.
entries.favorite: My jetpack not falling off once
entries.highlight: Trick-or-treated as an astronaut in a re-engineered jetpack that never fell off, alongside Ivy dressed as the moon.

entries.title: Where the bugs go in winter
entries.body: This morning there was frost on the grass for the first time, and when I looked for bugs after school, there were almost none, just like when I was seven. Back then I wondered where the bugs go in winter, and I thought they were hiding because they did not have jackets. Now I know the real answer, from my bug book and from my own observations. Some bugs, like roly polies, hide under logs where it is damp and warmer. Some, like Charlotte, leave eggs that wait until spring. Monarchs fly all the way to Mexico. Some beetles freeze almost solid and come back when they thaw. It is called overwintering. So I crossed that question off my oldest question list. It took two years. I flipped the old log, and there were the roly polies, huddled together like always.
entries.favorite: Answering a question from second grade
entries.highlight: Answered the question he asked at seven about where bugs go in winter, using his own observations and research on overwintering.

entries.title: Ivy makes the shopping list now
entries.body: Today me and Mom and Ivy went to the store for science ingredients. But this time Ivy made the list, all by herself, in her own letters. It said baking soda, vinegar, salt, and cabbage, with a drawing next to each one in case she spelled it wrong. She wanted to do the cabbage potion on her own. When the lady at the checkout asked what we were making, Ivy said a science experiment, and I am the scientist and he is my assistant. Mom laughed so hard. Two years ago, I made my first list for the egg drop parachute and a lady asked me the same question. Now Ivy is the one answering. I did not mind being the assistant. I think that is how it is supposed to go. Someday she will have her own lab too, maybe next to mine on the moon.
entries.favorite: Ivy checking things off her list
entries.highlight: Went science shopping with Mom and Ivy, who made her own list and announced that she was the scientist and Luke her assistant.

entries.title: I did science
entries.body: I wanted to do science so me and Mom went to the store to get ingredients. I made a list like I always do. Baking soda, a big jug of vinegar, dish soap, and red food coloring. We made a volcano with baking soda and vinegar, in the driveway so it would not get all over the lab. I put in the dish soap because I learned it makes the bubbles last longer. It fizzed up so high, higher than any volcano I ever made, and it went all over the driveway. Ivy did the countdown before I poured. I have been making volcanoes since I was seven and it is still fun every time. When I grow up I want my own lab, maybe on the moon. A real one, with a dome, like the clay one I made in art.
entries.highlight: Shopped with Mom for volcano ingredients and made his highest-fizzing baking soda volcano yet, still dreaming of a lab on the moon.

entries.title: If school was on the moon
entries.body: Today I thought about if school was on the moon. There is no gravity so kids would float in the air. Well, actually there is a little bit of gravity on the moon, about one sixth of Earth's, so kids would float really high when they jump and come down slowly. A kid floating would say can I join while he is floating, and he would float right into the tag game. Everybody would need helmets or they could not breathe, because there is no air. The school would be at the south pole, near the ice, like in my moon base research. And there would be windows where you could see Earth. I think Earth would look like a big blue marble. That would be the best view from any school ever.
entries.highlight: Imagined a school on the moon where kids float and need helmets, mixing his tag game with what he knows about lunar gravity.

entries.title: Drawing my perfect day
entries.body: I drew my perfect day. It has a pool, an ice cream shop a couple miles away, a candy sign with people waiting in line, and a lab on the moon. The ice cream shop only sells mint chip and bubblegum, for me and Ivy. The candy sign is giant and blinking, and the line goes around the block. The lab on the moon has a dome and a garden and Tidy-Bot cleaning up, and there is a telescope on top pointed back at Earth so I can see my house. I used my good markers and it took a long time. I want to send it to my parents so they know what to make. Mom said she can do the ice cream shop but the moon lab might take a while.
entries.highlight: Drew a picture of his perfect day with a pool, an ice cream shop, a candy sign and a lab on the moon to show his parents.

entries.title: The biggest game of tag
entries.body: At recess me and one friend started playing tag. It was me and Felix again on the big field. Then another kid came and said can I join? And we said yes. Then two more people said can I join? Then it was like the whole class. Then kids from the other fourth grade came too. The game kept getting bigger and bigger, so big that we had to make three people it at the same time. Even our teacher played for a minute. Ms. Alvarez ran after Wes and tagged him and everybody screamed. When I was in second grade I was too shy to even ask if I could join. Today the whole grade joined my game. Felix said I told you it would be the biggest game of tag ever.
entries.highlight: Started a game of tag with a friend at recess that grew to include the whole class and even the teacher.
